chand-bardai.name: Chand Bardai
chand-bardai.significance: Warrior-poet who died with Prithviraj Chauhan
chand-bardai.story:
When the sands of Rajputana turned crimson at sunset, it seemed as if the story of some hero were written in every grain. In that age of the 12th century—when swords were the very ink of history—a man was born whose voice was a weapon and whose weapon was a voice. He was Chand Bardai.

He was not born into an ordinary home, but into a tradition of valour and words. From childhood there was a different light in his eyes. While other boys learned only arms, Chand was mastering the power of words alongside weapons. His teacher would say—
"Words strike farther than the sword."

But he did not want to be only a poet—he wanted to witness the battlefield where valour is born.

As soon as he came of age, his path led him to Ajmer—to the court where the roar of the Chauhan dynasty echoed. There on the throne sat Prithviraj Chauhan—a symbol of prowess while still young.

When Chand first saw Prithviraj, the words came out of him on their own—
"This is not just a king; this is fire."

He became the court poet, but he also took part in the wars. When the kettledrums sounded, Chand did not only compose poetry—he put on armour, raised his sword, and rode onto the battlefield with his lord.

The first great clash took place on the field of Tarain. An army advancing from the west—led by Muhammad Ghori. His army was disciplined, swift and ambitious.

The field of Tarain filled with dust. The boom of kettledrums. The roar of "Har Har Mahadev!" Prithviraj in the front line. Chand behind him—but not merely as a spectator.

When the enemy struck head-on with cavalry, the Chauhan army wavered. Chand drew his sword.
"My king, today it is not words but weapons that will speak!"

Swords clashed. Arrows rained down. A cloud of dust and blood rose. Prithviraj challenged the enemy commander. Chand watched—the two face to face. Blow after blow. At last the Chauhan blow landed true. The first battle of Tarain ended in victory.

Returning to the court, Chand took up his pen. He shaped valour into words. So was born the poem that would echo for ages—the Prithviraj Raso. But it was not just a poem—it was a living picture of the battlefield.

But the current of history does not stand still. Ghori returned—and the second battle of Tarain was fought. This time fortune did not favour them. On the battlefield the Chauhan army broke. Prithviraj was taken prisoner.

Chand's heart burned. He saw his lord being bound in chains. But he did not turn back. He went too—not as a prisoner, but as a friend and poet.

*From here the story follows the legend of the Prithviraj Raso; history records that Prithviraj was put to death after Tarain, and that Ghori was assassinated in 1206.*

The court of Ghazni. Humiliation and challenge. Prithviraj had been blinded. But Chand's voice was still alive.

One day Ghori mocked—
"What can your king do now?"

Chand stepped forward.
"He can strike a target by sound alone."

Silence fell over the court. Slowly Chand recited a verse—
"Chaar baans chaubees gaj, angul asht pramaan…" (four bamboos, twenty-four yards, and eight finger-breadths…)

It was not just a poem—it was a signal. Prithviraj raised his bow. The string was drawn. The arrow flew.

A moment. Then a scream.

The arrow struck its target squarely. Ghori fell to the ground.

Chaos in the court. Soldiers running. Swords flashing.

Chand looked at Prithviraj.
"My king, the final moment has come."

The two looked into each other's eyes—years of friendship, memories of the battlefield, and the flame of honour.

Swords were raised. Enemies fell upon them from every side. Chand struck one last blow. Streams of blood flowed.

At last both fell to the ground—not in slavery, but with vengeance done.

Chand Bardai was not just a poet. He was the flame that proved words and weapons can go together. Through his poetry he made valour immortal, and through his blood he made it true.

Even today, when the wind blows across the sands of Rajputana, a voice echoes in it—
"Words are immortal… the Chauhans are immortal… Chand is immortal."

rawal-ratan-singh.name: Rawal Ratan Singh
rawal-ratan-singh.significance: Defender of Chittor against Alauddin Khilji
rawal-ratan-singh.story:
Chittor, standing firm in the harsh ranges of the Aravallis… the fortress where even stones took oaths, where the blood flowing on the ramparts wrote history. In that turbulent age of the 13th century—when the ambition of the Delhi Sultanate was advancing towards Rajputana—a ruler was born into the Guhila dynasty whose destiny would pass through fire and blood. He was Rawal Ratan Singh.

He was born within the high ramparts of Chittor. From childhood he saw it all—talk of war in the council halls, sentries posted on the bastions, and the echo of pride in the court. His teacher would tell him—
"A king's sword does not only protect the land; it protects honour."

The young Ratan Singh learned balance on horseback, a firm grip on the bowstring, fearlessness with the sword's edge. He was not just a warrior, but the guardian of the fortress. Every gate of Chittor, every secret passage, every bastion was known to him.

1303 CE. A vast cloud of dust rose on the horizon. The army of Alauddin Khilji, Sultan of Delhi, was advancing on Chittor. The roar of kettledrums, lines of countless soldiers, and a storm of ambition.

The council was grave. Some spoke of a treaty. Ratan Singh rose and said—
"Chittor was not made to bow."

The siege began. A vast camp outside the fortress. Catapults began to rain stones on the ramparts. The sky was covered in dust and smoke.

The first assault came at the eastern gate. The enemy advanced behind a line of heavy shields. Ratan Singh posted archers on the heights.
"Patience," he said, "let them come close."

As soon as they neared the gate, arrows rained from above. Boiling oil and stones fell. From below, Rajput warriors threw open the gate and charged out.
The cry of "Victory to Eklingji!" made the earth tremble. Swords met. Streams of blood flowed over the stones. The enemy fell back.

But the siege went on long. Supplies dwindled. Water was limited. Still Ratan Singh went to every bastion. He sat with the wounded soldiers.
"As long as we are here, Chittor lives," he would say.

The second assault came on the western rampart. This time the enemy chose the dark of night. Shadows danced in the torchlight. Ladders struck the wall. The enemy began to climb.

Ratan Singh himself reached the front line, sword in hand.
"Do not let the wall break!"

A fierce struggle broke out on the narrow rampart. Swords clashed so close that sparks flew. An enemy officer challenged him—
"Surrender, and your life will be spared!"

Flames blazed in his eyes—
"Chittor is greater than life!"

The two faced each other. Blow after blow. At last Ratan Singh's blow landed true. The officer fell. But the enemy's numbers were beyond counting.

The third and decisive moment came when a section of the rampart broke. A cloud of dust. The roar of kettledrums. The enemy poured inside.

Battle broke out in the streets within the fort. Ratan Singh organised the remaining army.
"Block the central passage!"

A wall of shields rose in the narrow lanes. There was no room for horsemen—this was a fight on foot. Swords clashed. Spears struck home. Blood flowed over the stones.

A spear drove into Ratan Singh's shoulder. He pulled it out and flung it away. His sword rose again. A second blow landed on his chest. He staggered, but did not fall back.

"Surrender!" the enemy called.

He replied—
"Guhilas do not bow!"

At last, amid many blows, he sank to his knees. His gaze went to the fortress's banner—still flying in the wind.

He fell to the ground—but his sword pointed forward.

That day Chittor was stained with blood, but its self-respect lived on. Ratan Singh's heroic death made the ramparts even more unshakeable.

He was not just a king. He was the flame that proved that even death is acceptable for the sake of honour.

Even today, when the winds of Chittor strike the ramparts, the clang of swords can be heard in them.

And in every echo a voice rings out—
"Chittor stands unshaken… the Guhilas are immortal."

jaitra-singh.name: Jaitra Singh
jaitra-singh.significance: Guhila king who resisted Delhi Sultanate
jaitra-singh.story:
When clouds thundered over the high ranges of the Aravallis, the ramparts of Chittor too seemed to roar in reply. In that age of the 13th century—when the Delhi Sultanate was pushing its power towards Rajputana—a boy was born in the lap of the Guhila dynasty who did not merely save Mewar, but expanded it too. He was Jaitra Singh.

1213 CE. Born in the royal palace of Chittor, this boy grew up not amid peace, but amid the sounds of struggle. Scattered wars on the borders, talk of strategy in the court, and news of the growing ambition coming from Delhi—this was his childhood.

From childhood Jaitra Singh understood the sword not merely as a weapon, but as a responsibility. With the first light of morning he would reach the stables. Balance on horseback, a firm grip on the bowstring, the straight thrust of the spear—his training was rigorous. But more than that, he was learning politics and strategy. He knew—if Mewar was to survive, defence alone was not enough; expansion was necessary too.

As soon as he took the throne he proclaimed in the court—
"Mewar will not remain a kingdom confined within its borders. Whoever comes against us will feel the strength of the Aravallis."

At that time the Delhi Sultanate was extending its influence over Rajputana. Its armies were equipped with heavy cavalry and mounted archers. But Jaitra Singh made the land his ally.

The first great clash came on the northern border. The Sultanate's army tried to fight on open ground. Instead of facing them head-on, Jaitra Singh drew them into the mountain passes. In the narrow way their vast army scattered. Arrows rained from above. Mewari horsemen crashed in from below.
The cry of "Victory to Eklingji!" made the valley tremble. Swords met. A cloud of dust and blood rose. In a short while the enemy fell back.

This victory was one not only of courage, but of strategy.

But Jaitra Singh did not stop there. He turned his gaze westward—to Nadol and Jalore, where the Chauhan dynasty held sway. He knew that if Mewar was to be strengthened, the surrounding powers would have to be balanced.

An army advancing on Nadol. On the open field the two armies faced each other. The kettledrums thundered. A vast cloud of dust rose.

The Chauhan horsemen struck first. They charged like lightning. The Mewari line wavered, but did not break. Jaitra Singh gave the signal—form a wall of shields in the centre, and spread the cavalry out on both sides.

The horsemen formed a crescent. The Chauhan army was trapped in the middle. Swords met. Spears struck home. A Chauhan commander challenged him—
"Turn back!"

Flames blazed in Jaitra Singh's eyes—
"Mewar does not retreat!"

The two faced each other. Blow after blow. At last his blow landed true. The commander fell. The Chauhan army began to fall back. Nadol's power weakened. Mewar's influence grew.

But the hardest struggle came when Delhi attacked again. This time the army was better organised. The roar of cannon and lines of heavy cavalry—the field trembled.

Jaitra Singh divided his army into three. Infantry in the centre, cavalry on both sides. After the first volley of the guns he gave the signal—
"Now!"

The horsemen crashed in like lightning. The sky rang with the clang of swords. The rain of arrows broke the enemy's lines. The battle went on for hours. In the end the Sultanate's army was forced to fall back.

Chittor remained safe. Mewar expanded.

But Jaitra Singh was not only a warrior of the battlefield. He had strategic forts built. Guard forts rose on the borders. Temple spires began to touch the sky. Learning and culture received patronage. Poets and scholars came to his court. The prestige of the Guhila dynasty spread far and wide.

One day someone in the court asked—
"Maharaj, why do you show equal zeal for both war and building?"

Jaitra Singh replied—
"Only when a kingdom's soul is strong do its borders hold."

For years he strengthened Mewar. Rajput lineages kept joining him. His valour and leadership made him not just a ruler, but a standard-bearer.

In his final years, when he stood on the ramparts of Chittor, he would gaze at the land stretching far away—expanded, secure and glorious. Within him was contentment that he had expanded Mewar not only in its borders, but in its influence too.

When his final moment came, the sun was setting. A red glow had spread over the walls of Chittor. He looked one last time at the fortress he had made unshakeable and expansive.

His breath stopped, but his saga came to live in the ramparts.

Jaitra Singh was not just a ruler. He was the resolve that proved the Guhila dynasty was not only a defender, but an expander too. He showed that when courage and strategy go together, no power can confine Mewar.

Even today, when the winds of the Aravallis strike the ramparts of Chittor, a voice echoes in them—
"Mewar stands unshaken… the Guhilas are immortal."

hammir-singh.name: Hammir Singh
hammir-singh.significance: Restored Mewar independence from Delhi Sultanate
hammir-singh.story:
When sunlight came down on the peaks of the Aravallis, even the broken ramparts of Chittor shone—as if, even after defeat, a challenge still remained in them. That was the 14th century, when Delhi's power overshadowed northern India and the soul of Mewar lay wounded. From that very wound a resolve was born… and the name of that resolve was Hammir Singh.

The early 14th century. A boy was born in the courtyard of the Sisodia dynasty. He came at a time when the shadow of subjugation lay over Chittor. The influence of the Delhi Sultanate had spread. Foreign banners flew on the ramparts. But the air of the Aravallis still carried the scent of rebellion.

From childhood the boy Hammir heard the story of defeat, but only one question rose within him—"Is this the end?"

His training was on the edge of the sword. With the first light of morning he would reach the stables. Balance on horseback, the sharp thrust of the spear, the steady bowstring—he was not just becoming a warrior; he was preparing for a revival.

By the time he came of age, his eyes held the flame that dares to free a conquered land. He learned that Delhi's power was weakening. Muhammad bin Tughlaq was entangled in his campaigns. The time was favourable—but courage was required.

He said in the assembly—
"Chittor was ours. And it will be ours again."

He reorganised the army. He set up outposts in the mountain passes. He brought the small Rajput strongholds together. "This is not only Mewar's war," he proclaimed, "it is a war of honour."

The first clash came on the frontier. A detachment from Delhi tried to crush the revolt. Hammir stopped them not on open ground, but in a mountain pass. Arrows rained from above. Horsemen crashed in from below. The valley trembled with the clang of swords. Within a few hours the detachment was defeated.

This was the beginning.

But Chittor was still under the Sultanate. The fortress was vast, but the enemy was inside. Hammir did not attack head-on. First he cut the supply routes. He took control of the trade roads leading to the fort. Small detachments raided by night. The enemy began to tire.

At last came the day when Hammir ordered the final assault.

It was dawn. The sun was crimson over the Aravallis. The Mewari army advanced on the fort. The kettledrums thundered. The cry of "Victory to Eklingji!" floated on the air.

The first blow fell on the main gate. The soldiers advanced behind a line of heavy shields. Arrows rained from above. Stones fell. But Hammir himself was in the front line. He spurred his horse and raised his sword—
"Today Chittor returns!"

Swords met. Blood flowed. An officer of the Sultanate challenged him—
"Surrender, and your life will be spared!"

Flames blazed in Hammir's eyes—
"Sisodias do not bow!"

The two faced each other. Blow after blow. At last Hammir's blow landed true. The officer fell.

The second stage was fought on the ramparts of the fort. Ladders struck the walls. Soldiers climbed up. A fierce fight on the narrow rampart. Swords so close that sparks flew. Hammir called out to his soldiers—
"Do not let the wall break!"

At last the gate opened. The Mewari army poured inside. Battle broke out in the streets. A cloud of dust and blood. The enemy began to fall back.

And then—the Sisodia banner flew once more over the ramparts of Chittor.

In that moment even the wind of the Aravallis seemed to pause. A conquered land had regained its freedom.

But Hammir did not stop there. He expanded the borders. He had strategic forts built. He strengthened the army. He organised the administration. Temple spires rose. Learning and culture received patronage. Scholars and poets began to come to the court.

He had understood—freedom does not endure by the sword alone; it endures through organisation.

Once someone in the court asked—
"Maharaj, you made the impossible possible. What was the secret?"

Hammir replied—
"Faith. As long as faith lives, the kingdom lives too."

With time Mewar became powerful again. The ramparts of Chittor were no longer just stone—they were a symbol of reawakening.

In his final years, when Hammir stood on the ramparts, he would gaze at the land stretching far away—free, secure and glorious. There was contentment in his eyes.

When his final moment came, the sun was setting. A red glow had spread over the walls of Chittor. He looked one last time at the fortress he had freed from subjugation.

His breath stopped, but the soul of Mewar had been revived.

Hammir Singh was not just a ruler. He was the flame of revival that proved defeat is not final. He fought not against death, but against slavery—and won.

Even today, when the winds of Chittor strike the ramparts, a voice echoes in them—
"Mewar is free… the Sisodias are immortal."

rana-lakha.name: Rana Lakha
rana-lakha.significance: Mewar king who expanded kingdom and built palaces
rana-lakha.story:
When the sun rose between the high arms of the Aravallis, the ramparts of Chittor glowed like golden fire. In that golden radiance, in the 14th century, a boy was born in the courtyard of the Sisodia dynasty whose destiny was not merely to sit on the throne, but to carry the kingdom to new heights—he was Rana Lakha.

He was born at a time when Mewar was determined to secure its independence. Outside powers had their eyes on Rajputana, and within, organisation was needed. From childhood the boy Lakha saw that Chittor was not just a fortress of stone—it was a stronghold of oaths.

With the first light of morning he would reach the stables. Balance on horseback, the sharp thrust of the spear, the precise movement of the sword—his training was rigorous. But more than that, he was learning the structure of the state. Sitting in the court, he listened to the nobles' discussions, learned the importance of the trade routes, and recognised the fragility of the borders.

By the time he came of age a clear vision had formed in his eyes—Mewar would not remain only on the defensive; it would expand.

As soon as he took the throne he reorganised the army. Cavalry bands were posted in different directions. Outposts were set up in the mountain passes. The infantry was trained to fight in dense lines of shields. He said—
"War is won not by courage alone, but by discipline."

The first great clash came on the southern border. The enemy army tried to enter through a narrow pass. Rana Lakha surveyed the ground. He posted his army on the heights and raised a wall of shields in the centre.

As soon as the enemy entered, arrows rained from above. Horsemen crashed in from below. The cry of "Victory to Eklingji!" made the valley tremble. Swords met. Blood flowed over the earth. In a short while the enemy fell back.

This victory was one not just of the battlefield, but of strategy.

The second battle was fought on the open plain. This time the enemy was greater in number and armed with mangonels. The crash of the mangonels shook the Mewari lines. Many soldiers fell. Smoke spread everywhere.

Rana Lakha ordered—
"After the first volley of stones, spread out, then strike together."

The mangonels were loosed. The smoke cleared. He raised his sword—
"Mewar!"

The horsemen burst forward like lightning. The field rang with the clang of swords. An enemy commander challenged him—
"Surrender!"

Flames blazed in his eyes—
"Sisodias do not bow!"

The two faced each other. Blow after blow. Strikes on the shield. At last Lakha's blow landed true. The commander fell. The enemy lines wavered.

With victory he adopted a policy of expansion. The borders were secured. The small strongholds were organised. Mewar's influence began to spread far and wide.

But Rana Lakha was not only a warrior—he was a builder too. He had grand palaces and forts built. The ramparts of Chittor were strengthened. Remarkable craftsmanship was imprinted on the chambers of the palace. Temple spires rose, their bells becoming a symbol of peace.

Scholars, poets and learned men began to come to his court. Learning received patronage. Manuscripts were collected. He had understood—a kingdom lives not only through its borders, but through its culture.

Once someone in the court asked—
"Maharaj, why do you show equal zeal for both war and building?"

Rana Lakha replied—
"Only when the fort is strong and the culture rich does the kingdom stand firm."

The third great struggle came when an organised army attacked Mewar's border. This time the battle was fought on the hill slopes. Rana Lakha adopted guerrilla tactics. Small detachments went out at night. Supply routes were cut. The enemy tired. In the final blow the Mewari army struck like a storm and the enemy fell back.

With time Mewar prospered. Green fields, lamps glowing in the temples, and steadfast sentries in the forts—all of it was the fruit of his foresight.

In his final years, when he stood on the ramparts, he would gaze at the land stretching far away—expansive, secure and glorious. There was contentment in his eyes.

When his final moment came, the sun was setting. A red glow had spread over the walls of Chittor. He looked one last time at the land he had expanded and strengthened.

His breath stopped, but Mewar's heartbeat had grown even stronger.

Rana Lakha was not just a ruler. He was the foundation that gave Mewar both expansion and prosperity. He proved that the Sisodia dynasty was great not only on the battlefield, but in architecture and culture too.

Even today, when the winds of the Aravallis strike the ramparts of Chittor, a voice echoes in them—
"Mewar stands unshaken… the Sisodias are immortal."

kanhad-dev-songara.name: Kanhad Dev Songara
kanhad-dev-songara.significance: Jalore ruler who resisted Alauddin Khilji
kanhad-dev-songara.story:
That harsh hill rising in the western arms of the Aravallis, on which the fortress of Jalore conversed with the sky—from there a flame rose in the 14th century. Surrounded by stone, that stronghold was not just a fort, but a sentinel of honour. And the lord of that sentinel was Kanhad Dev Songara.

Born into the tradition of the Songara line, Kanhad Dev learned from childhood that the land of the desert is kept safe by the sword. The narrow climbs of Jalore fort, its high bastions and its far-reaching watch—all of this lived in his eyes. He would ride around the hills on horseback, measure the depth of the passes, and memorise every footpath.

At that time Delhi's power was spreading across northern India. The Sultanate had its eye on the land of Rajputana. And when Alauddin Khilji's army advanced on Jalore in 1311, a sea of dust appeared on the horizon.

The council was grave. Some chiefs said—"The enemy is vast."
Kanhad Dev replied—"Our fort is high, and our resolve is higher still."

The siege began. Rows of camps below the fortress. Catapults began to rain stones on the ramparts. The walls shook, but held firm.

The first great assault came on the southern slope. The enemy began to climb behind a line of heavy shields. Kanhad Dev posted archers on the heights.
"Let them tire first," he said.

As soon as they were halfway up, arrows and stones rained from above. Boiling oil was poured down. Screams echoed through the valleys. Then a detachment rode out of the gate—Songara horsemen. Swords flashed like lightning. The enemy fell back.

But the Sultanate's army would not stop. A second wave came—this time in the dark of night. Ladders struck the ramparts. In the torchlight, shadows began to climb the walls.

Kanhad Dev himself reached the bastion.
"Do not let the wall break!" His voice rang out like a roar.

Swords clashed on the narrow rampart. So close that even the heat of breath could be felt. An officer challenged him—
"Surrender, and Jalore will be spared!"

Flames blazed in his eyes—
"Jalore is saved not by surrender, but by valour!"

The two faced each other. Blow after blow. Strikes on the shield. At last Kanhad Dev's blow landed squarely. The officer fell. But more soldiers were climbing from below.

The siege went on long. Water and grain began to run short. There was worry in the eyes of the citizens. But within the fort there was only one voice—"We will not bow."

At last a section of the rampart broke. A cloud of dust rose. The enemy poured in. Battle broke out in the streets. There was no room for horses—this was a fight on foot.

Kanhad Dev organised his remaining troops.
"Let no one advance towards the palace!"

A wall of shields formed in the narrow lanes. The enemy came like a wave. Struck. Broke. Came again.

A spear drove into his shoulder. Gritting his teeth, he pulled it out. His sword rose again. A second blow landed on his chest. He staggered, but did not stop.

"Surrender!" the voice came again.

He said for the last time—
"Songaras die; they do not bow."

And he charged again—wounded, but ferocious.

At last, from many blows, his body gave out. He sank to his knees. His gaze went to the banner of Jalore—still flying in the wind. A faint smile came to his lips.

He fell to the ground—but his sword still pointed forward.

That day Jalore was stained with blood, but its honour lived on. The sacrifice of Kanhad Dev Songara was not just a death—it was a vow that came to live in the stones.

He was not just a ruler. He was the flame that proved that for a Rajput, the kingdom and honour are one. He chose death, but not slavery.

Even today, when the winds of Jalore strike the ramparts of the fort, the clang of swords can be heard in them.

And in every echo a voice rings out—
"Jalore stands unshaken… the Songaras are immortal."

viramadeva.name: Viramadeva
viramadeva.significance: Jalore prince who refused Alauddin Khilji's terms and died in the siege of 1311
viramadeva.story:
**Viramadeva — the prince of Jalore who would not bend**

Viramadeva (Viramde) was the son of **Kanhad Dev Songara**, the Chauhan ruler of **Jalore**. He grew up in the years when **Alauddin Khilji** was bringing the great Rajput fortresses down one after another: Ranthambore in 1301, Chittor in 1303, Siwana in 1308.

**The story of Firoza**

The 15th-century poem *Kanhadade Prabandh*, written by the poet **Padmanabha** in 1455, tells how Viramadeva went to Delhi as a hostage or envoy, and how the Sultan's daughter **Firoza** fell in love with him. The Sultan offered her hand, but Viramadeva refused, for to accept would have meant giving up his faith and his people. The poem treats this refusal as one of the causes of the final war. Historians regard the episode as legend, but it shows how Jalore remembered its prince.

**The siege of Jalore, 1311**

Alauddin's army, led by **Kamaluddin Gurg**, besieged Jalore. After a long siege, betrayal opened the way into the fort. Kanhad Dev fell fighting. According to the *Kanhadade Prabandh*, Viramadeva was crowned in the burning fort and ruled for only three and a half days, then led the last charge and was killed. The women of Jalore performed **jauhar**.

**Memory**

The poem says that Viramadeva's head was carried to Delhi, and that Firoza, grieving, gave her own life. Whatever the truth of that ending, Viramadeva is remembered in Jalore as the prince who chose death over submission, at the side of his father.

kunwar-kanh-singh.name: Kunwar Kanh Singh
kunwar-kanh-singh.significance: Mewar prince who died defending Chittor

Swords met. Spears struck home. Blood flowed over the stones. Kanh Singh himself was in the front line. A spear drove into his shoulder. He pulled it out and flung it away. His sword rose again. A second blow landed on his chest. He staggered, but did not fall back.

"Surrender!" the enemy called.

He replied—"Sisodias do not bow."

At last, from many blows, his body gave out. He sank to his knees. His gaze turned towards the banner of Chittor—still flying in the wind. A faint smile came to his lips.

He fell to the ground—but his sword still pointed forward.

That day the land of Chittor was stained with blood, but its self-respect lived on. Kanh Singh's heroic death made the ramparts even more unshakeable.

He was not just a young prince. He was the flame that proved even youth can change the course of history. He chose death, but not slavery.

Even today, when the winds of Chittor strike the ramparts, the clang of swords can be heard in them.

And in every echo a voice rings out—
"Chittor stands unshaken… the Sisodias are immortal."

rao-jodha.name: Rao Jodha
rao-jodha.significance: Founder of Jodhpur city and Mehrangarh Fort
rao-jodha.story:
When the sun rises over the blazing sands of the Thar, its first ray turns the rocks crimson—as if the earth itself were repeating a vow of war. In 1416 CE, in the lap of that same desert, in the palaces of the Rathore dynasty, a boy was born who did not merely raise the sword—he carved out a city. He was Rao Jodha.

He was born into splendour, but the times were of struggle. Marwar was consolidating its independence. Scattered power, small strongholds and the ambitions of neighbouring states—there was challenge in every direction. From childhood the boy Jodha saw that the throne was not just a right, but a summons to the battlefield.

As soon as morning came he would reach the stables. He mastered balance on horseback and struck precisely with the spear at a gallop. The sword's edge had become part of his wrist. But sharper still was his vision—he read the land. To him the desert was not barren, but an opportunity.

By the time he came of age he had understood that Marwar needed not just defence, but a permanent centre—a stronghold that would become the symbol of Rathore power. His gaze fell on a high rock—a hill rising under the blue sky that could command the land for miles around.

"Here," he said, "we will build our stronghold."

And from that resolve was born Mehrangarh—Mehrangarh Fort.

Walls rose, cut from the rock. Bastions began to touch the sky. Iron spikes were set into the gates. This was not just a fort—it was a declaration that Rathore power was unshakeable.

But a foundation is not laid with stones alone. The first great clash came when a powerful neighbouring chief challenged the newly founded stronghold. The ground was flat, but dunes spread far and wide. Jodha posted his army behind the dunes. The front line offered light resistance and began to fall back.

The enemy advanced—believing victory was easy. Just then horsemen burst out from behind the dunes. The cry of "Rathore!" made the air tremble. Swords met. A cloud of dust and blood spread everywhere. Jodha himself was in the front line. He parried a chief's blow with his shield and with his counter-stroke pierced his chest. In a short while the resistance broke.

This victory was as important as the foundation of Mehrangarh itself.

The second clash was fiercer. This time the enemy was greater in number and armed with gunpowder. On the open field the two armies faced each other. The kettledrums sounded. The roar of the guns shook the earth. Many Rathore soldiers fell.

Jodha ordered—"After the first volley, scatter, then strike together."

The guns were fired. The smoke cleared. He raised his sword—"Marwar!"

The horsemen burst forward like lightning. The desert trembled with the clang of swords. An enemy commander challenged him—"Surrender!"

Flames blazed in Jodha's eyes—"Rathores do not bow!"

The two faced each other. Swords clashed, sparks flew. At last Jodha's blow landed true. The commander fell. The enemy fell back.

But Jodha was not only a warrior. He was a builder. In the shadow of Mehrangarh a city began to take shape—Jodhpur. Settlements grew, markets opened, trade routes were secured. Outposts were built to protect the water sources. Temple spires rose, where the sound of bells became a sign of peace.

The third great battle was fought in a mountain pass. The enemy was advancing along a narrow way. Jodha posted soldiers on the heights. As soon as the enemy entered, arrows and stones rained from above. Horsemen crashed in from below. The heavy army was trapped in the narrow way. It was a victory of strategy.

Scholars, poets and learned men began to come to his court. Learning and culture received patronage. Jodhpur became a centre not only of the battlefield, but of knowledge and art too.

Once someone in the court asked, "Maharaj, why did you build this fort at such a height?"

Jodha replied, "So that generations to come will know—Rathore power does not stand only on the ground; it touches the sky."

With time Marwar expanded. The influence of the Rathore dynasty spread far and wide. The name of Jodhpur began to echo in the politics of Rajputana.

In his final years, when he stood on the ramparts of Mehrangarh, he would look at the city spread out below—blue settlements, temple spires, safe roads. All of it was the fruit of his resolve.

When his final moment came, the sun was setting. A red glow had spread over the walls of Mehrangarh. He looked one last time at the stronghold he had carved out of the rock.

His breath stopped, but Jodhpur lived on.

Rao Jodha was not just a ruler. He was the craftsman who carved a city out of the desert. He proved that the Rathore dynasty could establish its power not only with the sword, but through building too.

Even today, when the wind passes over the ramparts of Mehrangarh, a voice echoes in it—
"Jodhpur is immortal… the Rathores are immortal."

ranmal-rathore.name: Ranmal Rathore
ranmal-rathore.significance: Rathore king who expanded Marwar territories
ranmal-rathore.story:
When hooves struck the sands of the Thar, they did not merely raise dust—they announced that the desert had awakened. In the late 14th century, in the lap of that same desert, in the courtyard of the Rathore dynasty, a boy was born whose very destiny was expansion—he was Ranmal Rathore.

He was born amid splendour, but the atmosphere was one of struggle. Marwar was strengthening its borders. Small strongholds, scattered power, and the ambitions of neighbouring states—there was challenge in every direction. From childhood Ranmal saw that the throne was not just a right, but a call to war.

With the first light of morning he would reach the stables. Gripping the horse's mane he mastered balance, and practised with the spear on the open plain. The bowstring did not tremble in his fingers. To him the sword's edge was not a weapon, but a resolve. But sharper still was his vision—he read the land, understood the routes, and saw the lines of the future.

By the time he came of age he had decided—Marwar would not remain only on the defensive; it would expand.

The first great clash came near the border. A neighbouring chief challenged the power of Marwar. The ground was flat, but dunes spread far and wide. Ranmal hid his army behind the dunes. The front line offered light resistance and began to fall back.

The enemy advanced—believing victory was easy. Just then horsemen burst out from behind the dunes. The cry of "Rathore!" made the air tremble. Swords met. A cloud of dust spread everywhere. Ranmal himself was in the front line. He parried a chief's blow with his shield and with his counter-stroke pierced his chest. In a short while the enemy fell back.

This was not just a victory—it was a declaration that Marwar's borders would no longer stand still.

The second clash was more complicated. This time the confrontation was with the power of Mewar. Narrow passes among the Aravalli hills, high ramparts and a seasoned army. Ranmal understood that a direct attack could prove costly.

He divided his army into three. The infantry stood in the centre forming a wall of shields, cavalry on both sides. He ordered—"Take control of the mountain roads. Cut the supplies."

The battle began. Arrows rained from the hills. Ranmal signalled his horsemen to spread out. As soon as the enemy tired, he raised his sword—"Marwar!"

The horsemen burst forward like lightning. The Aravallis trembled with the clang of swords. The struggle was fierce. In the end both sides fell back, but Ranmal had proved that Marwar was no longer only a desert power, but a centre of the politics of Rajputana.

The third and decisive battle was fought on the open plain. The sun was overhead. The kettledrums sounded. A cloud of dust was rising. The enemy was greater in number.

Ranmal arranged his army in dense lines. The roar of the guns shook the earth. Many soldiers fell. But he ordered—"Do not break ranks!"

After the next volley of the guns he gave the signal—"Now!"

Horsemen crashed in from both sides. Swords met. An enemy commander challenged him—"Surrender!"

Flames blazed in Ranmal's eyes—"Rathores do not bow!"

The two faced each other. Swords clashed, sparks flew. At last Ranmal's blow prevailed. The commander fell. The enemy lines wavered.

With victory he had forts built. Strong forts rose on the borders. Outposts were built to protect the water sources. Trade routes were secured. Temples were built, where the sound of bells became a symbol of peace. Scholars, poets and learned men began to come to his court. Marwar became not only a battlefield, but a land of culture too.

Once someone in the court asked, "Maharaj, where does expansion end?"

Ranmal replied, "Wherever honour is safe, there lies the border."

With time Marwar's power grew. The influence of the Rathore dynasty spread far and wide. Neighbouring states now regarded him not just as a ruler of the desert, but as an influential leader of Rajputana.

In his final years, when he stood on the ramparts of his fort, he would gaze at the land stretching far away—forts, settlements, temples and safe roads. All of it was the fruit of his resolve.

When his final moment came, the sun was setting. A red glow had spread over the sand. He looked one last time in the direction of Marwar—the land he had expanded and strengthened.

His breath stopped, but Marwar's power lived on.

Ranmal Rathore was not just a ruler. He was the flame of expansion that lifted the Rathore dynasty out of the desert and made it a leader in the politics of Rajputana. He proved that power lies not only in defence, but in expansion and organisation too.

Even today, when the winds of the Thar strike the walls of the forts, a voice echoes in them—
"Marwar is immortal… the Rathores are immortal."

rao-bika.name: Rao Bika
rao-bika.significance: Founder of Bikaner city and kingdom
rao-bika.story:
In the north-western expanse of the Thar, where every grain of sand burns like fire under the sun, a boy was born in 1438 CE—a boy who would turn the emptiness of the desert into a kingdom. He was Rao Bika.

Born into the tradition of the Rathore dynasty, Bika saw from childhood that power comes not only through inheritance, but through courage and vision. He grew up within the walls of Marwar, but his eyes stayed fixed on the distant horizon—on the sands where no banner yet flew.

Balance on horseback, the precise thrust of the spear, control of the sword's edge—these were his daily routine. But more than that, he read the land. He had come to understand that the desert was not merely desolate—it was an opportunity.

By the time he came of age he had decided—he would establish his own territory. He would found a new branch of the Rathore dynasty.

It began with struggle. When he entered that part of the desert where small chiefs and tribes were each defending their own borders, he was challenged. The first battle took place on a flat plain where dunes spread far and wide.

Bika posted his army behind the dunes. The front line offered light resistance and began to fall back. The enemy took this for weakness. As soon as they advanced, horsemen burst out from behind the dunes. The cry of "Rathore!" made the air tremble. Swords met. A cloud of dust spread everywhere. Bika himself was in the front line. He parried a chief's blow with his shield and with his counter-stroke ripped open his chest. In a short while the resistance broke.

This was not just a victory—it was the first brick of a foundation.

He planted his banner on that land. Slowly settlements began to grow. Outposts were built near the water sources. Trade routes were secured. And then—a city began to take shape. It was Bikaner.

But a city is not founded by name alone. It needed walls—strong and unshakeable. Bika ordered a fort to be built. High ramparts rose, bastions were built, iron spikes were set into the gates. That fort, later known as Junagarh, was not just a structure of stone—it was a symbol of Rathore resolve.

The second great clash came when a powerful neighbouring chief challenged the rise of Bikaner. This time the battle was fought on open ground. The kettledrums sounded. Horsemen faced each other. The desert trembled with the clang of swords.

Bika divided his army into three. The infantry stood in the centre forming a wall of shields, cavalry on both sides. He ordered—"Stop the first blow, then encircle them."

The enemy attacked fiercely. The wall of shields stopped them. As soon as their momentum slowed, Bika raised his sword—"Now!"

Horsemen crashed in from both sides. The encirclement was complete. Within a few hours the enemy lines scattered. It was a decisive victory.

But Bika was not only a warrior. He was a builder. He had temples built. He gave patronage to learning in the city. He gave protection to merchants. Poets and scholars began to come to his court. Bikaner was no longer just a fort—it was becoming a centre of culture.

Once someone in the court asked, "Maharaj, how is prosperity possible in the desert?"

Bika replied, "Where there is courage, the road to prosperity makes itself."

The third and hardest struggle came when an organised army from afar camped on Bikaner's border. This time the enemy was greater in number. The plain was wide. The smell of gunpowder hung in the air.

Bika surveyed the ground. He turned his army towards a narrow way. As soon as the enemy entered, arrows rained from above. Horsemen crashed in from below. Swords met. Blood sank into the sand. The enemy fell back.

Bikaner remained safe.

With time the city prospered. From the ramparts of the fort one could see far into the distance. The bells of the temples and the clang of weapons echoed side by side. Bika's vision gave the desert an identity.

In his final years, when he stood on the heights of the fort, he would look at the city spread out below—settlements, markets, temples, military outposts. All of it was the fruit of his foresight.

When his final moment came, the sun was setting. A red glow had spread over the walls of Junagarh. He said softly, "The land has been established."

His breath stopped, but Bikaner lived on.

Rao Bika was not just a ruler. He was the builder of the desert—who gave the Rathore dynasty permanent roots in a new land. He proved that valour lies not only in war, but in founding too.

Even today, when the winds of Bikaner strike the ramparts of Junagarh, a voice echoes in them—
"The Rathores are immortal… Bikaner is immortal."

rao-shekha.name: Rao Shekha
rao-shekha.significance: Founder of Shekhawati region and dynasty
rao-shekha.story:
On that land of Rajputana, where sand and rock seemed to struggle against each other, a boy was born in 1433 CE—a boy who would shape not only his own destiny, but the identity of an entire region. He was Rao Shekha.

He was born into the tradition of the Kachwaha dynasty. There was courage in his blood, but the circumstances were not simple. New strongholds were being founded across Rajputana. Small forts were rising, new chiefs were carving out their territories. Power was being established not by the sword alone, but by foresight.

From childhood the boy Shekha understood that the land of the desert belongs only to those who can water it with their sweat and blood. Balance on horseback, spear practice on the open plain, a firm grip on the shield—this was his daily routine. But he was not only becoming a warrior; he was becoming a builder too.

By the time he came of age his gaze had settled on that stretch of desert where there was as yet no strong authority. There were scattered settlements, unsafe roads and instability. He resolved—a new territory would be born here. A land that would carry his identity.

The beginning was not easy. The surrounding chiefs were busy defending their own borders. Some saw his rise as a challenge. The first clash came on the border. The ground was flat, but dunes spread far and wide. Shekha hid his army behind the dunes. The front line offered light resistance and began to fall back.

The enemy advanced—believing victory was easy. Just then horsemen burst out from behind the dunes. The cry of "Kachwaha!" made the air tremble. Swords met. A cloud of dust and blood spread everywhere. Shekha himself was in the front line. He parried a chief's blow with his shield and with his counter-stroke ripped open his chest. In a short while the enemy fell back.

This was not just a victory—it was a declaration that a new power was being born.

But a territory cannot be established by war alone. With a strategic eye he began building forts. Forts rose on high ground, from where watch could be kept far and wide. Outposts were built near the water sources, to keep supplies safe. Every fort was a symbol not only of defence, but of control.

The second great clash came when a powerful chief attacked the newly established territory. This time the battle was fought on open ground. The kettledrums sounded. Horsemen faced each other. The earth trembled with the clang of swords.

Shekha divided his army into three. The infantry stood in the centre forming a wall of shields, cavalry on both sides. He ordered—"Do not advance until you get the signal."

The enemy attacked fiercely. The wall of shields stopped the first blow. As soon as the enemy tired, Shekha raised his sword—"Now!"

Horsemen crashed in from both sides. The ring closed. Within a few hours the enemy lines broke. The victory was decisive. Now it was no longer easy to challenge his leadership.

Shekha did not only win land; he won the trust of the people. He secured the trade routes. He gave protection to the settlements. He had temples built, where the sound of bells gave a sign of peace. Learning was encouraged. Scholars, poets and learned men began to come to his court.

On one occasion a chief in the court asked, "Maharaj, why are you building so much? The forts are enough."

Shekha replied, "Forts give protection, but culture gives identity. If the identity is strong, the kingdom is unshakeable."

The third and fiercest struggle came when an outside power tried to stop the rise of Shekhawati. This time the enemy was greater in number. The plain was wide. A cloud of dust was rising.

Shekha surveyed the ground. He turned his army towards a narrow way. As soon as the enemy entered, arrows rained from above. Horsemen crashed in from below. The heavy army was trapped in the narrow way. Swords flashed. Blood flowed. The enemy fell back.

From that day Shekhawati became not just a name, but an identity.

With time a chain of forts arose. Temple spires began to touch the sky. Trade flourished. People began to feel safe. Shekha's court became not just a place for planning war, but a centre of culture too.

In his final years, when he stood on the ramparts, he would gaze at the territory stretching far away—forts rising amid the sand, lamps burning in the villages, sounds coming from the temples. All of it was the fruit of his foresight.

When his final moment came, the sun was setting. A red glow had spread over the walls of the forts. He said softly, "The land has been established."

His breath stopped, but Shekhawati lived on.

Rao Shekha was not just a ruler. He was a builder—who gave the Kachwaha dynasty roots in a new land. He proved that valour lies not only on the battlefield, but in building too.

Even today, when the winds of Shekhawati strike the forts, a voice echoes in them—
"The foundation is immortal… the Kachwahas are immortal."

maharani-hansa-bai.name: Maharani Hansa Bai
maharani-hansa-bai.story:
*Historical note: Hansa Bai, the Rathore queen of Rana Lakha and mother of Rana Mokal, is a historical figure, but the battles and acts of government described here are not recorded in the sources.*

When the first light of morning fell on the rocks of the Aravallis, it did not touch only the stones—it touched the soul of Mewar. In the 15th century that same soul took form in a woman who treated the crown not as an ornament, but as a responsibility. She was Maharani Hansa Bai.

She was born amid Rajput splendour, but her personality was not confined to splendour. From childhood she saw that behind the glitter of palaces lay the complexity of politics. Hushed consultations in the council halls, dust rising on the borders, and the balancing of the nobles—all of this was part of her education. She became accomplished not only in the scriptures, but in strategy too.

When she became Maharani of Mewar, the kingdom was struggling not only with outside enemies but with internal imbalance too. Disputes among the nobles, small clashes on the frontier, and the challenges of the revenue system—amid all this she established herself not merely as a queen, but as an administrator.

When a difficult question arose in the court, her voice was calm but decisive. "A kingdom is kept safe by the sword," she would say, "but prosperity comes from justice and order." She had the tax system reformed. The excessive burden on farmers was reduced, so that green would return to the fields and the granaries would stay full. Regular arrangements were made for soldiers' pay and supplies, so that their morale on the battlefield would stay firm.

Once news came from the frontier—the enemy army had camped near a pass. Worry spread through the court. Some chiefs were talking of a direct attack. The Maharani sent for a map. She looked at the lie of the hills and said, "Let them come into the pass. Strike from the heights. When their horses tire, then use the sword."

Following her advice the army laid an ambush in the narrow way. When the enemy came in, arrows and stones rained from above. Horsemen crashed in from below. In a short while the danger passed. The soldiers said among themselves—"The queen's eye can read even the battlefield."

But her contribution was not limited to war. She had the forts repaired and the water sources secured. Temples were built, their walls bearing remarkable craftsmanship. She gave patronage to learning. Gurukuls received grants, manuscripts were collected. Poets, scholars and musicians came to her court. Mewar became not only a land of swords, but a land of culture too.

On one occasion a dispute arose in the court. Some nobles wanted more power. The situation was tense. Maharani Hansa Bai entered the assembly. "If we break from within," she said, "the enemy outside will swallow us. Mewar's strength lies in unity."

Her firmness quieted the dispute. She set out clear responsibilities in the administration. The system of courts was strengthened. Regular accounts began to be kept of the kingdom's income and expenditure. Discipline and balance gave the kingdom stability.

But one more test remained. Suddenly, one night, the enemy stormed the fort. The sound of kettledrums broke the sleep. Chaos broke out on the ramparts. The Maharani herself reached the bastion. In the torchlight her face was calm but radiant.

"Put out the torches," she ordered, "the darkness will confuse them."

In the dark the enemy lost its way. The Mewari soldiers attacked without warning. Swords met. Within a few hours the enemy fell back. There was pride in the soldiers' eyes—their queen was not only the guardian of the palace, but a guide on the battlefield too.

With time Mewar prospered. Green fields, the sound of bells in the temples, and the discussions of scholars in the court—all of it was the fruit of her foresight. She had understood that a kingdom lives not only through its borders, but through culture and order.

Even in her final years she remained active in the court. She taught the heirs—"The weight of the crown is borne more by wisdom than by the sword."

When her final moment came, the sun was setting over the Aravallis. A red glow had spread over the ramparts. She looked one last time at the forts she had strengthened, the temples she had built, and the court where learning and statecraft went hand in hand.

Her eyes closed, but her name was inscribed in the heartbeat of Mewar.

Maharani Hansa Bai was not just a queen. She was the wisdom that gave the sword its direction. She proved that a woman could stand not only behind the curtain, but at the centre of the state. Her legacy lives on today in the ramparts, in the bells of the temples, and in the stability of the administration.

Even today, when the winds of the Aravallis strike the walls of Chittor, a voice echoes in them—
"Mewar is prosperous… Mewar stands unshaken."

rao-nara.name: Rao Nara
rao-nara.story:
*Historical note: The identity of Rao Nara and the battles described here cannot be confirmed from historical sources. Read this story as legend, not history.*

When the sun rose over the golden sands of the Thar, its rays gleamed on the edges of swords. That was the 15th century—when the shadows of forts lay long over the land of Rajputana and war was not only about borders, but about honour. In that age a general was born in the lap of the Rathore dynasty who made his name the echo of the battlefield—he was Rao Nara.

He was born into struggle more than splendour. The land of Marwar was harsh, and its people harsher still. From childhood he saw that the walls of a fort are not just stone—they are vows. As his father placed a sword in his hand he had said, "Rathore blood shines bright only when tempered in war."

The boy Nara would reach the stables as soon as morning came. Mastering balance on horseback, he learned to fall and rise again. The bowstring did not tremble in his fingers. His spear thrust was straight and fast. But sharper still was his vision—he could read the battlefield before the battle began.

It was a time when Mewar's power was at its height. That power was led by Rana Kumbha—a symbol of strategy and valour. The relationship between Marwar and Mewar carried notes of both cooperation and conflict, but one thing was clear—unity was needed against enemies both foreign and internal.

The young Nara was given the responsibility of general. It was not just a post—it was an oath to stand in the front line on the battlefield. He reorganised the army. The horsemen were given light armour, so that they could move like a storm across the desert. The infantry was trained in dense lines of shields. He said, "War is won not by strength alone, but by discipline."

The first great battle took place on the frontier. The enemy army crossed the desert and attacked. The ground was flat, but there were high and low dunes as far as the eye could see. Rao Nara hid his army behind the dunes. The front line offered light resistance and began to fall back.

The enemy advanced—believing victory was easy. Just then arrows and spears rained from behind the dunes. Horsemen crashed in from both sides. The cry of "Rathore!" made the air tremble. Swords met. A cloud of dust and blood spread everywhere. Rao Nara himself was in the front line. He parried an enemy commander's blow with his shield and with his counter-stroke pierced his chest. In a short while the enemy fell back.

This was not just a victory—it was a sign that the desert still burned.

The second clash took place in a mountain pass, where the enemy was greater in number. Rao Nara surveyed the ground. He posted soldiers above and left the narrow way below open.

As soon as the enemy entered, stones and arrows began to rain from above. Horsemen crashed in from below. The heavy army was trapped in the narrow way. The cannon became useless. It was a victory of strategy.

But the decisive battle was still to come.

On the open field the two armies faced each other. The sun overhead, the smell of gunpowder in the air. Rana Kumbha himself was present. The kettledrums sounded. The roar of the guns shook the earth.

Rao Nara signalled his troop—"After the first volley, scatter, then strike together."

The guns were fired. Many soldiers fell. The smoke cleared. He raised his sword—"Marwar!"

The horsemen burst forward like arrows. Swords met. Spears struck home. Blood flowed over the earth. An enemy officer challenged him—"Surrender!"

Flames blazed in Rao Nara's eyes—"Rathores choose death, not slavery!"

The two faced each other. Swords clashed, sparks flew. At last Rao Nara's blow prevailed. The officer fell.

But the enemy's numbers were vast. He began to be surrounded on every side. A spear drove into his shoulder. He pulled it out and flung it away. His sword rose again. A second blow landed on his chest. He staggered, but did not fall back.

Looking towards Rana Kumbha, he called out—"My lord, go forward! We are the wall!"

And he truly became a wall. He held back the enemy line with his own body. His blows were slowing, but the flame in his eyes did not go out.

At last, from many blows, his body gave out. He sank to his knees. His gaze went to the banner flying over the battlefield. A faint smile came to his lips.

He fell to the ground—but his sword still pointed forward.

The battle ended, but Rao Nara's sacrifice became immortal. Rana Kumbha said, "Generals like this are the foundation of a kingdom."

Rao Nara was not just a general. He was the resolve that showed that Rathores do not only rule—they also give their lives on the battlefield. His strategy, his courage, and his final decision—to accept death—were engraved in the sands of the desert.

Even today, when the wind of the Thar blows, the clang of swords can be heard in it.

And in every echo a voice rings out—
"The Rathores are immortal."

rana-raimal.name: Rana Raimal
rana-raimal.story:
When clouds thundered among the hills of the Aravallis, their echo struck the ramparts of Chittor and seemed to make a single declaration—Mewar stands unshaken. As the heartbeat of that steadfastness, in the 15th century, a boy was born in the palaces of the Sisodia dynasty who would one day turn scattered power into an organised iron fist. He was Rana Raimal.

His birth was not merely the arrival of a prince—it was a ray of hope in an age of struggle. Mewar at that time was also battling challenges from within. Disputes among the nobles, clashes on the borders, and the watching eyes of neighbouring powers—the kingdom needed a firm hand.

From childhood the boy Raimal saw that the throne was not just a right, but a symbol of unending war. As soon as morning came he would reach the stables. Gripping the horse's mane to master balance, practising the sword's edge on the open plain, strengthening his grip on the shield—this was his daily routine. But more than that, he listened carefully to the discussions in the court. He began to understand that winning wars was not enough—the kingdom also had to be organised from within.

By the time he came of age a clear resolve could be seen in his eyes. He saw that Mewar's strength was scattered. In different strongholds the nobles were entangled in their own dominions. He decided—first the walls within had to be strengthened.

As soon as he sat on the throne he first reorganised the army. Cavalry troops were given separate responsibilities. Outposts were set up in the mountain passes. The infantry was trained in dense lines of shields. He said, "War is won not by valour alone, but by discipline."

The first great struggle was against an internal revolt. Some nobles were challenging the unity of the kingdom. Raimal did not attack directly. First he cut off their supplies and offered them a chance to make terms, and then, when the revolt grew—he struck decisively.

On the open field the two armies faced each other. The sun was overhead. The kettledrums sounded. Swords came out of their scabbards. Raimal spurred his horse—"Mewar!"

The horsemen charged. The earth trembled with the clang of swords. The rebel army resisted fiercely, but before the disciplined lines they began to waver. Raimal himself was in the front line. He parried a chief's blow with his shield and with his counter-stroke ripped open his chest. Within a few hours the revolt was put down.

Now the outside challenge stood before him. A neighbouring power prepared to attack the frontier. This time the enemy was greater in number. The ground was flat, but there was a range of hills to the west.

Raimal surveyed the ground. He divided his army into three. The front line would offer light resistance, and two troops would hide behind the hills.

The battle began. The enemy advanced. The Mewari front line seemed to fall back. The enemy took this for weakness and came deep inside. Just then arrows and stones rained from the hills. Horsemen crashed in from both sides. The cry of "Victory to Eklingji!" echoed through the air. The enemy lines scattered.

This victory was one not of the sword alone, but of strategy.

The third and decisive battle was fiercer. This time the enemy came with gunpowder and cannon. The first roar of the guns shook the ramparts. Many soldiers fell. Smoke spread everywhere.

Raimal ordered—"Do not break ranks! After the next volley, scatter, then charge together."

The guns were fired. The smoke cleared. He raised his sword—"Now!"

The horsemen burst forward like lightning. Swords met. Spears struck home. An enemy commander challenged him—"Surrender!"

Flames blazed in Raimal's eyes—"Sisodias do not bow!"

The two faced each other. Swords clashed, sparks flew. At last Raimal's blow landed true. The commander fell. The enemy fell back.

But Raimal was great not only in war. He had temples built and forts repaired. The water sources were secured. Learning and culture received patronage. Scholars came to his court, and poetry and the scriptures were discussed. He had understood—a kingdom lives not only through its borders, but through its culture.

He put the tax system in order. Farmers were given protection, so that the land would stay fertile. The army was given regular pay and training. He gave the nobles clear responsibilities—the unity of the kingdom came first.

Time passed. Mewar's strength had been organised. Enemies now thought twice before attacking. A wind of peace began to blow through the valleys of the Aravallis—but behind that peace stood a firm leadership.

Even in his final years the same flame was in Raimal's eyes. He taught his heirs—"Power does not endure by the sword alone; it endures through organisation."

When his end drew near, the sun was setting. A red glow had spread over the ramparts. He looked one last time towards Chittor—at the walls he had strengthened.

His breath stopped, but Mewar's heartbeat had grown even stronger.

Rana Raimal was not just a ruler. He was the foundation on which the valour of generations to come would stand. He proved that power lies not only on the battlefield, but in organisation and administration too.

Even today, when the winds of the Aravallis strike the ramparts of Chittor, a voice echoes in them—
"Mewar is organised… Mewar is immortal."

kunwar-prithviraj-mewar.name: Kunwar Prithviraj Mewar
legends: Restored Toda for Tara Bai's father
kunwar-prithviraj-mewar.story:
**Kunwar Prithviraj — the 'flying' prince of Mewar**

Prithviraj was the eldest son of **Rana Raimal** of Mewar and the elder brother of **Sangram Singh**, the future **Rana Sanga**. He was famous for the speed of his raids, and Mewar's tradition calls him **Udana Prithviraj**, the 'flying' Prithviraj.

**The quarrel of the brothers**

Tradition tells that Prithviraj, Sanga and their brother **Jaimal** consulted a priestess to learn which of them would rule Mewar. When she pointed to Sanga, Prithviraj attacked him in anger, and Sanga lost an eye in the fight. Sanga fled, and lived for years in hiding.

**Tara Bai and Toda**

The best-known story of Prithviraj is that of **Tara Bai**, the daughter of **Rao Surtan Solanki**, who had been driven out of **Toda**. She vowed to marry only the man who won back her father's lands. Prithviraj led a daring night attack, recovered Toda, and married Tara Bai. Tradition links her name with **Taragarh**, the fort of Ajmer.

**His death**

Prithviraj did not die in battle. He quarrelled with his brother-in-law, **Jagmal**, the ruler of **Sirohi**, over Jagmal's ill-treatment of Prithviraj's sister. After a reconciliation, Jagmal gave him poisoned sweets as he left, and Prithviraj died on the way home, near **Kumbhalgarh**, in the first years of the 16th century, before his father. Tara Bai is said to have become sati with him.

**Legacy**

Prithviraj's early death opened the way for Sanga, who became one of Mewar's greatest rulers.

maharani-rani-sona.name: Maharani Rani Sona
maharani-rani-sona.story:
*Historical note: No queen of Mewar named Rani Sona is found in the historical record. Read this story as legend, not history.*

Among the hills of the Aravallis, where clouds thundered against the stones and the ramparts glowed like golden fire at sunset, Mewar saw the birth in the 15th century of a queen whose strength lay not in the sword alone, but in wisdom and resolve. She was Rani Sona—a name that echoed equally in the peace of palaces and the roar of the battlefield.

She was born into the dignity of the Sisodia dynasty. From childhood she began to understand the gravity of the royal court, the subtlety of counsel and the balance of the state. While other princesses were absorbed in music and adornment, Sona sat in the assembly and paid attention to the tax system, military supply and the state of the borders. In her eyes there was not only gentleness, but brilliance too—the kind of brilliance that marks a leader.

When she became Maharani of Mewar, the times were not easy. Small clashes on the borders, the ambitions of neighbouring states, and the challenge of maintaining political balance within the court—amid all of this she established herself not merely as a queen, but as a guardian.

When a dispute arose in the royal court, her voice was calm but firm. "A kingdom can be won by the sword," she would say, "but stability comes from justice." She reformed the tax system. The excessive burden on farmers was reduced, so that the land would prosper and the granaries stay full. Regular arrangements were made for soldiers' pay and supplies, so that the army's morale would stay high.

But her role was not limited to administration. She ordered the repair and expansion of the forts. The ramparts were strengthened, the water sources secured. Once news came from the frontier that a neighbouring power had massed troops on the border. Worry spread through the court.

Rani Sona sent for a map. She studied the position of the hills and passes. "No direct attack," she ordered. "Set up outposts on the hills. Keep the supply routes safe. Wear the enemy down, then strike."

Following her instructions the army took up positions in the narrow passes. When the enemy advanced, arrows and stones rained from above. Horsemen crashed in from below. Within a few days the danger passed. Her strategy became the talk of the court—a queen who could read the land.

Her second great test came when the spark of an internal revolt flared. Some nobles were discontented. They demanded tax exemptions and more powers. The situation could have become serious. But instead of the sword, the queen chose the path of dialogue. She called an assembly.

"Mewar is not just a throne," she said. "It is the shared heritage of us all. If we break from within, the enemy outside will swallow us."

Her firmness and balance quieted the revolt. She introduced new policies in the administration—the nobles' responsibilities were made clear and the system of courts was strengthened. Regular accounts began to be kept of the kingdom's income and expenditure.

But she was known not only as an administrator. She was a patron of art and culture too. Poets, craftsmen, musicians and scholars came to her court. Temples were built, their walls bearing remarkable craftsmanship. She gave patronage to gurukuls for education. Manuscripts were collected. Mewar became not only a land of battle, but a land of learning too.

On one occasion, when an envoy came from a neighbouring state, he said mockingly—"Can a queen run a kingdom?"

Rani Sona smiled and replied—"Running a kingdom takes courage, and courage does not distinguish between woman and man."

Her very presence was the balance of the court. She oversaw preparations for war and laid the foundation stones of temples. She made provision for soldiers' families, so that while fighting on the battlefield they would not have to worry about home. This was foresight—war is won not by the sword alone, but by morale.

Once there was a sudden attack on the frontier. The enemy struck in the dark of night. Chaos broke out on the ramparts of the fort. The queen herself reached the bastion. She addressed the soldiers—"The rampart is made of stone, but the strength is you!"

Her presence doubled the soldiers' zeal. She gave orders—"Put out the torches; let them lose their way in the dark." The enemy lost its bearings. The Mewari soldiers attacked without warning. Within a few hours the danger passed.

Time went by. Mewar prospered. The bells of the temples and the clang of weapons rang out side by side. Art, music and architecture gave the kingdom a new identity. But behind every decision was a resolute mind—Rani Sona.

Even in her final years she remained active in the court. She taught her heirs—"A kingdom is not only its borders, but its culture too. As long as the culture lives, the kingdom lives."

When her end drew near, the sun was setting over the Aravallis. A red glow had spread over the ramparts. She looked one last time at the fort—at the temples and bastions into which her labour and love had gone.

Her eyes slowly closed, but her name came to live in the heartbeat of Mewar.

Maharani Rani Sona was not just a queen. She was the strength that showed that ruling is not only war, but balance. She proved that a woman is not merely an ornament of the palace, but can set the course of the kingdom.

Even today, when the wind of the Aravallis strikes the temple bells, a voice echoes in it—
"Mewar is prosperous."

medini-rai.name: Medini Rai
medini-rai.significance: Rajput chief and ally of Rana Sanga
medini-rai.story:
**Medini Rai — the lord of Chanderi**

**Medini Rai** was a **Purbiya** Rajput who rose to great power in the Sultanate of **Malwa**. As chief minister of **Sultan Mahmud Khalji II**, he filled the court with his own Rajput followers, until the Sultan, fearing him, turned against him.

**With Rana Sanga**

Medini Rai turned to **Rana Sanga** of Mewar. In **1519**, at the battle of **Gagron**, Sanga defeated Mahmud Khalji II and took him prisoner. Sanga gave Medini Rai the fortress of **Chanderi** and its lands, and Medini Rai became one of Mewar's most loyal allies.

**Khanwa, 1527**

When Sanga led the Rajput confederacy against **Babur**, Medini Rai brought his Purbiya contingent to **Khanwa** (March 1527). The Rajputs were defeated by Babur's guns and cavalry tactics. Medini Rai survived the battle and returned to Chanderi.

**The siege of Chanderi, 1528**

In January 1528 Babur marched on **Chanderi**. He offered Medini Rai another fort in exchange for Chanderi. Medini Rai refused. Babur's guns battered the walls. When the end came, the women of Chanderi performed **jauhar**, and Medini Rai and his men came out to fight their last battle. Chanderi fell on **29 January 1528**, and Medini Rai died with his men.

**Memory**

Babur's own memoirs describe the ferocity of the last fight at Chanderi. Medini Rai is remembered as the ally who kept faith with Sanga to the end, even after Khanwa.

haridas-tomar.name: Haridas Tomar
haridas-tomar.significance: Sanganer chief who fought in Mughal wars
haridas-tomar.story:
*Historical note: No Tomar chief named Haridas of Sanganer is found in the historical record. Read this story as legend, not history.*

Sanganer, lying between the lands of Amber and Dhundhar… where once the sound of artisans' hammers echoed, in the 16th century the clang of swords also made its name. Shifting power in northern India, growing Mughal might, and the restless winds of Rajputana—amid this upheaval was born a Tomar chief who turned his small state into a wall. He was Haridas Tomar.

He was born not amid splendour, but amid vigilance. The fort of Sanganer was not vast, but the banner that flew on its ramparts was one of self-respect. In the tradition of the Tomar line he was taught from childhood—"The land may be small, but not one's pride."

The boy Haridas would reach the stables before sunrise. Balance on horseback, the straight stroke of the sword, a firm grip on the shield—practising all of these was his daily routine. But he was not only becoming a warrior; he was becoming a leader. Sitting in the assembly he listened to the elders—politics, diplomacy, and the price of a decision in a moment of crisis.

At that time an empire was expanding in the north. The Mughal army was organised, armed with cannon and gunpowder. Many small chiefs either bowed or were bound by treaties. But this young chief of Sanganer was different. He said—"Our land is small, but our vow is great."

When he became chief of Sanganer, he had two choices before him—surrender or struggle. He chose struggle.

The first great battle was fought on Sanganer's border. A Mughal detachment was advancing. The ground was flat, but to the west lay a chain of small hills. Haridas surveyed the ground. He divided his army into three. The front line would offer light resistance, and two troops would hide behind the hills.

As the morning sun climbed, the battle began. The roar of the guns shook the earth. Many Tomar soldiers fell. The front line seemed to fall back. The Mughal army advanced—believing victory was easy.

Just then arrows and bullets rained from behind the hills. Horsemen crashed in from both sides. The cry of "Tomar!" echoed through the air. Swords met. A cloud of dust spread everywhere. Haridas himself was in the front line. He parried a Mughal officer's blow with his shield and with his counter-stroke ripped open his chest. The enemy lines wavered. Within a few hours they began to fall back.

This victory was the breath of life for Sanganer.

But the enemy did not sit still. The second clash was fiercer. This time the Mughal army came with heavy cannon. They began to batter the ramparts of the fort. Stones broke, dust rose. Haridas understood that simply holding the walls was not enough.

By night he adopted guerrilla tactics. Small detachments were sent out, which cut the enemy's supply routes. One night he went out himself with twenty horsemen. They made a sudden raid on the Mughal camp. Swords flashed like lightning. The powder store caught fire. The explosion threw the camp into chaos. Haridas gave the signal—"Back!" and they vanished into the darkness.

This war was one not only of strength, but of morale.

The third and decisive struggle took place on the open plain. The two armies faced each other. The kettledrums sounded. The guns roared. Dust and smoke filled the air.

Haridas arranged his army in a dense line of shields. Cavalry on both sides. He said—"After the first volley, scatter, then charge together."

The guns were fired. Many soldiers fell. The smoke cleared. Haridas raised his sword—"Sanganer!"

The horsemen burst forward like arrows. Swords met. Spears gleamed. Blood flowed over the earth. A Mughal commander challenged him—"Surrender! Your life will be spared!"

Flames blazed in Haridas's eyes—"Life without honour is worthless!"

The two faced each other. Swords clashed, sparks flew. At last Haridas's blow landed true. The commander fell. But the enemy's numbers were beyond counting. He began to be surrounded on every side.

A spear drove into his shoulder. He pulled it out and flung it away. His sword rose again. A second blow landed on his chest. He staggered, but did not fall back.

"Surrender!" the enemy called again.

He replied—"Tomars do not bow."

At last, from many blows, his body gave out. He sank to his knees. His gaze went towards the fort of Sanganer—where the banner was still flying. A faint smile came to his lips.

He fell to the ground—but his sword still pointed at the enemy.

Haridas Tomar was not just the chief of a small state. He was the wall that showed resolve matters more than size. His strategy, his courage, and his final decision—to accept death—became immortal in the soil of Sanganer.

Even today, when the winds of Dhundhar blow, the clang of swords can be heard in them. The fort of Sanganer still stands—as if repeating that hero's vow.

And in every echo a voice rings out—
"The Tomars are immortal."

silhadi-singh.name: Silhadi Singh
silhadi-singh.significance: Tomar Rajput chief of Raisen who changed sides at Khanwa and died against Bahadur Shah of Gujarat
silhadi-singh.story:
**Silhadi — the lord of Raisen**

**Silhadi** (Salahdi) was a **Tomar** (Puarbiya) Rajput chief who rose in the service of the Sultans of Malwa and became the master of **Raisen**, **Bhilsa** and **Sarangpur** in eastern Malwa. As the Malwa Sultanate weakened, he became one of the most powerful men in the region.

**Khanwa, 1527**

Silhadi joined **Rana Sanga** in the great Rajput confederacy against **Babur**. At the battle of **Khanwa** in March 1527, according to most accounts, he went over to Babur's side in the middle of the battle. His desertion is counted among the causes of Sanga's defeat, and Rajput tradition has never forgiven it.

**The siege of Raisen, 1532**

After Khanwa, Silhadi returned to Malwa. In **1532** Sultan **Bahadur Shah of Gujarat**, who had conquered Malwa, turned on him. Silhadi was seized and pressed to give up his faith, while the Gujarat army besieged **Raisen**. His wife, **Rani Durgavati**, a daughter of Rana Sanga, led the women of Raisen into the fire of **jauhar**. Silhadi and his remaining kinsmen died fighting in the last charge.

**A divided memory**

Silhadi's story is one of the most complex of the age. He is remembered both for the betrayal at Khanwa and for the jauhar and saka of Raisen, five years later.

rani-karnavati.name: Rani Karnavati
