rani-karnavati.significance: Queen of Rana Sanga and regent of Mewar who led the jauhar of 1535
rani-karnavati.story:
**Rani Karnavati — the regent of Chittor**

**Rani Karnavati** (Karmavati) was a queen of **Rana Sanga** and the mother of two future rulers of Mewar, **Vikramaditya** and **Udai Singh II**. After Sanga's death in 1528, Mewar was weakened by the defeat at Khanwa, and when the young and unpopular **Vikramaditya** came to the throne, Karnavati became the real guardian of the state.

**The threat from Gujarat**

In **1534–35**, **Sultan Bahadur Shah of Gujarat**, who had already conquered Malwa, besieged **Chittor**. Many of Mewar's nobles, angry with Vikramaditya, had stayed away. Karnavati appealed to them in the name of Mewar's honour, and they returned to defend the fort.

**The rakhi to Humayun**

A famous tradition, recorded in later accounts, says that Karnavati sent a **rakhi** to the Mughal emperor **Humayun**, asking him as a brother to come to her aid. Humayun set out, but he did not reach Chittor in time.

**The second saka of Chittor**

Bahadur Shah's artillery breached the walls. Before the fort fell, the two young princes were sent away to safety in **Bundi**. In **March 1535**, Rani Karnavati led the women of Chittor into the fire of **jauhar**, and the men, led by **Bagh Singh** of Deolia, rode out to die in the **saka**. It was the second great saka of Chittor.

**Legacy**

Karnavati's son Udai Singh survived to become Maharana and the father of **Maharana Pratap**. Her choice to send the princes away while she herself stayed is remembered as the act that saved the line of Mewar.

rao-maldeo-rathore.name: Rao Maldeo Rathore
rao-maldeo-rathore.significance: The most powerful Rathore ruler of his age, who fought Sher Shah Suri at Sammel
legends: Recovered Jodhpur after Sher Shah's death
rao-maldeo-rathore.story:
**Rao Maldeo — the most powerful Rathore of his age**

Maldeo was born on **5 December 1511**, the son of **Rao Ganga** of Marwar. He became ruler of Marwar in **1532** and reigned for thirty years. Persian historians called him the most powerful ruler in Hindustan of his time.

**Building a great Marwar**

Maldeo expanded Marwar in every direction. He took **Nagaur**, **Ajmer**, **Merta**, **Sojat**, **Jalor** and **Siwana**. In **1542** he defeated and killed **Rao Jaitsi** of **Bikaner** at the battle of **Sohaba** and occupied Bikaner. At its height his kingdom reached from the Thar to the borders of Mewar and Delhi.

**Humayun and Sher Shah**

In 1542 the fugitive Mughal emperor **Humayun** came towards Marwar hoping for Maldeo's help, but the help did not come, and Humayun turned away. Soon after, Maldeo faced a far greater danger: **Sher Shah Suri**, the Afghan ruler of Delhi.

**Sammel, 1544**

In January 1544 the two armies faced each other near **Sammel** (Giri-Sumel). Sher Shah, uncertain of victory, had forged letters planted to make Maldeo believe that his own chiefs were about to betray him. Maldeo withdrew in suspicion. His loyal commanders **Jaita** and **Kumpa** refused to retreat and attacked Sher Shah's army with a few thousand men, dying almost to the last man. Sher Shah is said to have remarked that he had nearly lost the empire of Hindustan for a handful of millet.

**Recovery and death**

Sher Shah occupied Jodhpur, but after his death in 1545 Maldeo recovered his capital and much of his kingdom. He died a natural death on **7 November 1562**.

rao-chandra-sen-rathore.name: Rao Chandra Sen Rathore
rao-chandra-sen-rathore.significance: Rathore king who continued resistance against Mughals
legends: Fought on from the hills of Marwar
Called the forgotten hero of Marwar
rao-chandra-sen-rathore.story:
**Rao Chandrasen Rathore — the forgotten hero of Marwar**

Chandrasen was born on **16 July 1541**, a younger son of **Rao Maldeo**. When Maldeo died in **1562**, Chandrasen was chosen as ruler over his elder brothers **Ram** and **Udai Singh**. His brothers turned against him and sought help from **Akbar**, and Chandrasen faced enemies both within his family and from the empire.

**The loss of Jodhpur**

In **1565** a Mughal army under **Husain Quli Khan** besieged **Jodhpur**, and Chandrasen was forced to give up his capital. He withdrew to **Bhadrajun**.

**The Nagaur durbar, 1570**

In **1570** Akbar held a court at **Nagaur**, and many Rajput rulers came to submit. Chandrasen came, but when he saw the terms, he left without submitting. His brother Udai Singh stayed and accepted Mughal service. Akbar later gave Jodhpur to **Rai Singh of Bikaner** to govern.

**War from the hills**

For the rest of his life Chandrasen fought from the hills and forts of Marwar: from **Bhadrajun**, from **Siwana**, and from the Aravalli hills around **Sojat** and **Saran**. He lost his forts one by one, regained some, and never accepted Akbar's authority. He fought the same kind of war that **Maharana Pratap** was fighting in Mewar, and some historians call him Pratap's forerunner.

**His death**

Chandrasen died on **11 January 1581** at **Sachiyap**, in the hills of Saran, not in battle. Some accounts say he was poisoned by a treacherous follower. After his death his brother **Udai Singh** became ruler of Marwar as a Mughal ally.

**Memory**

Because Marwar's later rulers descended from Udai Singh, Chandrasen was long neglected by the court chroniclers. Today he is remembered as the **forgotten hero of Marwar**.

kunwar-uday-singh.name: Maharana Udai Singh II
kunwar-uday-singh.significance: Maharana of Mewar, founder of Udaipur and father of Maharana Pratap
legends: Saved as a child by Panna Dhai
kunwar-uday-singh.story:
**Maharana Udai Singh II — the founder of Udaipur**

Udai Singh was born on **4 August 1522**, the youngest son of **Rana Sanga** and **Rani Karnavati**. His childhood was shaped by danger. Before the siege of Chittor in 1535, he was sent away to safety in Bundi.

**Saved by Panna Dhai**

In **1536**, the usurper **Banbir** murdered Udai Singh's brother, **Vikramaditya**, and came to kill the young prince too. His nurse, **Panna Dhai**, put her own son in Udai Singh's bed. Banbir killed the child, and Panna escaped with Udai Singh hidden in a basket, carrying him to the safety of **Kumbhalgarh**.

**The recovery of Chittor**

Udai Singh was crowned at Kumbhalgarh in **1537**, and with the support of Mewar's nobles he drove out Banbir and recovered **Chittor** around **1540**.

**The founding of Udaipur**

Udai Singh understood that Chittor, on its open hill, was exposed to the great armies of the age. In **1559** he founded a new city in the protected valley of the Girwa hills, beside **Lake Pichola**: **Udaipur**.

**Akbar's siege of Chittor**

When **Akbar** marched on Chittor in **1567**, Udai Singh, on the advice of his council, withdrew to the hills, leaving the fort in the hands of **Jaimal Rathore** and **Patta Chundawat**. Chittor fell in **February 1568** after a heroic defence. Udai Singh's decision has been both criticised and defended ever since: it cost Chittor, but it kept the ruler of Mewar free.

**His death**

Udai Singh died at **Gogunda** on **28 February 1572**. He named his son Jagmal as heir, but the nobles crowned **Maharana Pratap**.

jaimal-rathore.name: Jaimal Rathore
jaimal-rathore.significance: Chittor defender who died defending the fort
jaimal-rathore.story:
*Historical note: This profile is about the same warrior as Jaimal Mertia (Jaimal Rathore of Merta), who led the defence of Chittor in 1567–68. Tradition says he was wounded by a shot from Akbar himself.*

When the sun's rays fell on the harsh rocks of the Aravallis, it was not only the stones that shone—they revealed the oath of history. The ramparts of Chittor, on which blood had flowed countless times, were awaiting yet another storm in the 16th century. Amid the roars of that age a warrior was born whose very destiny was to become a wall—he was Jaimal Rathore.

Born into the tradition of the Rathore dynasty, Jaimal heard the sound of war drums from childhood. The swords hanging on the walls of his home were not merely decoration; they were living symbols. His mother told him tales of heroes as she rocked him in her lap, and his father, placing a sword in his hand for the first time, said, "This is your breath. As long as it keeps rising, you are alive."

From childhood Jaimal learned not to play, but to prepare. With the first light of morning he would climb the bastion of the fort and gaze at the plain spread out below. He knew—one day that same plain would fill with an enemy army. His balance on horseback was remarkable. He could stand on a galloping horse and throw a spear. The bowstring did not quiver in his fingers. His gaze was steady—as if he could see the result before every blow.

Meanwhile, in the north, power was expanding. A vast empire, heavy cannon, countless soldiers—and at the centre of it all sat an ambitious ruler—Akbar. His gaze was on Chittor. This fortress was not only strategic, but symbolic. It had to be made to bow.

When the Mughal army marched on Chittor, Jaimal Rathore had already taken charge of the fortress's defence. He may not have been old, but there was more resolve in him than experience. He said in the council, "The walls are made of stone, but the strength is ours. If the rampart falls, we will fall with it—but we will not bow."

The siege began. Rows of Mughal camps spread far and wide. For the first time the rumble of cannon shook the ramparts. Stones broke, a cloud of dust rose. But Jaimal, standing on the bastion, was unshaken.

The first assault came on the western wall. A section was weakened by constant bombardment from the guns. As soon as the breach widened, the Mughal infantry advanced. With cries of "Allahu Akbar!" they were setting up ladders.

Jaimal gave the signal—"Archers, aim!"

Arrows rained down. Many soldiers fell below. But their numbers were beyond counting. Some reached the wall. Jaimal himself stepped forward. He struck a soldier's shield with his sword, then dropped to one knee and struck at his legs. He fell. Another climbed up—Jaimal shoved him back with his shield. As he fell, his scream dissolved into the air.

The fighting lasted an hour. At last the Mughal army fell back. But this was only the beginning.

Jaimal understood that direct combat could not last long. He adopted a new strategy. Using tunnels and secret passages from inside the fort, small parties began to be sent out at night. They would reach the Mughal guns and damage the wheels, set the powder stores on fire, and come back. These guerrilla tactics unsettled the enemy.

One night, when the moon was half full and there was a chill in the air, Jaimal himself went out with twenty soldiers. They raided the enemy's forward guns. Swords flashed like lightning. Cutting down the guards, they hacked through the wheels of the guns. A sudden explosion threw the Mughal camp into turmoil. Jaimal smiled—"War is won not only on the walls, but in the mind too."

But the siege was long. Supplies were dwindling. Tension was rising within. Then one day preparations for a decisive assault were seen. The Mughal army deployed huge cannon in front. Under constant bombardment a section of the wall collapsed. A cloud of dust rose. Through the broken stones the enemy's lines came into view.

Jaimal was wounded—a fragment of stone from a cannon shot had struck his thigh. But he refused to fall back. He could not stand, so his kinsman Kalla Rathore lifted him onto his own shoulders. From there, with a sword in each hand, he fought on.

"Chittor!" his roar rang out.

The soldiers charged. The battlefield by the broken wall began to smoulder. Swords clashed. Shields shattered. Spears struck home. Blood flowed over the stones.

A Mughal officer saw him and challenged him—"Jaimal! Surrender!"

Fire blazed in Jaimal's eyes—"Rathores do not fear death!"

He fought on from Kalla's shoulders. Despite his wounded leg he advanced. Their swords clashed. Sparks with every blow. At last Jaimal's blow landed true—the officer fell.

But the enemy surged in from every side. A musket fired. Smoke rose. The bullet pierced his body. He staggered, but did not fall. He gripped his sword even tighter.

"Keep fighting!" his voice rang out.

The soldiers fought even more fiercely. But the numbers and means against them were too great. Another blow. Then another. At last Jaimal sank to his knees. His gaze rose to the sky beyond the broken wall. The sun was crimson—as if it had itself come down to join the battle.

He fell to the ground—but the sword did not leave his hand.

That day Chittor was bathed in blood. The flames of jauhar rose. The ramparts were covered in smoke. But the name of Jaimal Rathore was engraved in the stones—as a defender who held the fortress until his last breath.

Even today, when the wind blows over the walls of Chittor, the clang of swords can be heard in it. At sunset a red glow covers the stones—as if the memory of that day had come alive again.

Jaimal Rathore—he was not just a warrior. He was the moment when even walls turn to blood and fight. He was the roar that tells us forts are kept safe not by stones, but by lives.

And the valleys of the Aravallis still echo—
"Chittor is immortal."

patta-sisodia.name: Patta Sisodia
patta-sisodia.story:
When the first ray of the sun touched the ramparts of Chittor at the foot of the Aravallis, it was not a golden glow that shone on the stones, but a vow. This was not just a fort—it was the soul of Mewar. And to defend that soul, in the 16th century, a youth was born whose years were few but in whose heart a fierce flame burned—he was Patta Sisodia.

He was born into the dignity of the Sisodia dynasty. From childhood he was told—"Chittor is not just a fortress of stone; it is the blood of our ancestors." There was a stern love in his mother's eyes. His father, placing a sword in his hand, said—"This is raised not only against the enemy, but in defence of your own self-respect."

From childhood Patta learned not to play among the ramparts of the fort, but to train. Early in the morning he would climb the bastions and gaze at the distant horizon—as if wanting to recognise the enemy's approach before it came. In the stables he raced with the horses, then practised with shield and sword in the open courtyard. His arms were not yet fully grown, but in his gaze was a firmness rare even among seasoned warriors.

Those were stormy times. In the north, the Mughal empire's expansion kept growing. Its eyes were fixed on one fort after another. Chittor—it was a challenge in itself. And the one who stepped forward to take up that challenge was a ruler of vast ambition—Akbar.

The walls of Chittor were high, the moats deep, and the people within unshakeable. But the Mughal army was boundless in numbers and means—cannon, gunpowder, heavy cavalry. When the siege drew near, Patta Sisodia was still young. But youth did not lessen his resolve; rather, there was a fierceness in it.

A council was held inside the fort. Veteran chiefs, priests, soldiers—all gathered. Patta stepped forward and said, "If Chittor falls, it will fall over our lives. The word surrender is not in our language."

The siege began. The Mughal guns spat fire at the ramparts. Stones broke, clouds of dust rose. Inside the fort the women and children went to places of safety. But Patta stood on the bastions—shield raised, sword gleaming.

The first great assault came at the southern gate. The Mughal army weakened the wall with heavy cannon and then sent the infantry forward. The cry of "Allahu Akbar!" rose.

Patta signalled his soldiers—"Arrows ready!"

As soon as the enemy came close, the rain of arrows began. Many soldiers fell. But their numbers were vast. They set up ladders and began to climb the wall. Patta himself stepped forward. He kicked down a ladder. He cut off the hand of a soldier climbing up. A stream of blood ran down the wall.

The fighting went on for several hours. The sun set, but the struggle did not stop. At last the Mughal army fell back—the first assault had failed.

But the siege was long. Days turned into weeks. Supplies began to run short. But morale held firm. Patta adopted a new strategy. He began sending small troops out at night—raiding the Mughal camps and returning. These guerrilla attacks unsettled the enemy.

One night the moon was hidden in the clouds. Patta rode out of the fort with twenty horsemen and attacked the enemy's powder store. Swords flashed like lightning. Cutting down the guards, they set it on fire. The explosion threw the Mughal camp into chaos. He returned swiftly. This was not just courage, but strategy—weakening the enemy's strength from within.

But at last the day came when the Mughal army prepared a decisive assault. Under constant bombardment from the guns, a section of the rampart had broken. A cloud of dust rose. The vast army advanced.

Inside the fort the flames of jauhar had already risen. The women had entered the fire—as the last defence of their honour. The flames of that fire kindled an even fiercer flame in the men's eyes.

Patta Sisodia put on the saffron robe. His mother applied the tilak to his forehead. "Victory or a hero's death," she said, "but do not bow."

The broken section of the rampart had become a battlefield. The Mughal army was forcing its way in. Drums were beating. Dust, smoke and screams—all together created a terrible scene.

Patta raised his sword—"Chittor!"

His roar filled the soldiers with new energy. They charged. Swords met. Spears struck home. Blood flowed over the stones.

A Mughal officer challenged him—"Young man, surrender! Your life will be spared!"

Fire blazed in Patta's eyes—"Sisodias choose honour, not life!"

He spurred his horse and charged straight at the officer. Their swords clashed. Sparks flew. For a few moments they were evenly matched. Then Patta's blow landed true—the officer went down.

But the enemy surged in from every side. A spear drove into his shield. He flung the shield away and gripped his sword with both hands. His body bore many wounds, but he did not fall back. He brought down soldier after soldier.

Amid the dust and blood he was like a storm. But their numbers were beyond counting. A blow from behind struck his shoulder. He staggered, yet still struck back. Then another blow.

At last he sank to his knees. His sight was blurring. He looked towards the broken rampart—where the Sisodia banner was still flying. A faint smile came to his lips.

He fell to the ground—but his sword still pointed at the enemy.

That day Chittor was soaked in blood. But the name of Patta Sisodia was engraved in the stones. He was not just a young defender—he was the moment when youth challenged death.

Even today, when the sun sets on the ramparts of Chittor, its rays turn red—as if remembering the blood of that day. The clang of swords can still be heard in the air.

And in every echo a voice rings out—

Patta Sisodia.

hakim-khan-sur.name: Hakim Khan Sur
hakim-khan-sur.significance: Commander of Maharana Pratap who fought at Haldighati
hakim-khan-sur.story:
Even when the winds blew dry and hot through the valleys of the Aravallis, there was a stubbornness in them—a refusal to bow. In the fire of that stubbornness, in the turbulent times of the 16th century, a warrior was born in whose veins Afghan valour and the honour of Rajputana flowed side by side—he was Hakim Khan Sur.

He was born into the tradition of the Sur dynasty, the line that had once raised its banner over the thrones of northern India. But times had changed. The Mughal empire kept spreading its iron claws. Many dynasties had either been defeated or were on the path of compromise. But there were some souls who accepted death before defeat. Hakim Khan was one of those souls.

From childhood he was surrounded by the gleam of swords and the neighing of horses. He grew up in the camps of the Sur dynasty—where military training began with the first light of morning. When a sword was placed in his palm for the first time, his teacher said, "This is not just an edge of iron; it is the oath of your existence."

He became skilled in horsemanship. He raced across the open plains, cutting through the wind, and practised shooting arrows standing on horseback. His eyes were sharp—able to read the lines of the battlefield, the enemy's moves and the pulse of time. But he was not only becoming a warrior; he was becoming a strategist too. He learned that war is won not by strength of arm alone, but by strength of spirit and mind.

Meanwhile, on the throne of Mewar sat the lion whose very name meant rebellion—Maharana Pratap. He was the last unshakeable wall against Mughal expansion. When Hakim Khan heard the saga of Pratap's struggle, the flame within him blazed even higher. He decided—he would fight under the banner that stood for freedom, whatever its faith or lineage.

When he reached Mewar, many eyes were weighing him up. An Afghan warrior in the army of Rajputana? But Pratap saw in his gaze a loyalty that goes beyond blood. "Mewar needs you," Pratap said. And from that day Hakim Khan Sur was not just an ally, but a commander.

He introduced new war techniques into the army. Light cavalry troops, a policy of swift attack and immediate withdrawal, strikes on the enemy's supply routes—he taught the soldiers that victory comes not from numbers, but from speed and coordination. He also paid special attention to the use of cannon and muskets, to offset the Mughal army's technical edge.

The first great clash took place in a frontier region, where a Mughal detachment was advancing with supplies. The ground was flat, but surrounded by small hills. Hakim Khan surveyed the ground and made a plan. He divided the army into three—two troops hid behind the hills, and the third began a light attack from the front.

As soon as the Mughal army focused on the troop in front, arrows and bullets suddenly rained from both sides. The horses stampeded. Hakim Khan himself was in the front line. "Forward!" his roar rang out. Swords clashed. A Mughal chief struck at him, but he swung his shield to stop the blow and with his counter-stroke struck at his neck. In a short while the enemy's supplies had been destroyed.

This was not just a skirmish; it was a message that Mewar was still alive.

But history's harshest test was yet to come—Haldighati.

The morning of 18 June 1576. The first ray of the sun fell on the yellow earth of Haldi. Before them was the vast sea of the Mughal army—lines of elephants, heavy cavalry, rows of cannon. On the other side the army of Mewar—fewer in number, but fierce in spirit.

Hakim Khan Sur was given charge of the vanguard. He looked at his soldiers—Rajputs, Bhils, Afghans—all under one banner. "Today's battle is not about faith or lineage, but freedom," he said. There was such firmness in his voice that the soldiers' hearts blazed.

The kettledrums sounded. The Mughal guns spat fire. The earth shook. Many Mewari soldiers fell. Amid the dust and smoke Hakim Khan gave the signal—"Scatter!" The soldiers spread out, and the next volley was wasted. Then he raised his sword—"Now!"

The horsemen burst forward like arrows. "Victory to Eklingji!" and "Allahu Akbar!" rose together—a remarkable unity. Swords met. Spears gleamed. Streams of blood began to flow.

Hakim Khan crashed straight into the Mughal vanguard. An elephant came at him. He turned his horse and struck at the elephant's mahout with his spear. The mahout fell, and the elephant went out of control. He used that chaos to push his troop deep inside.

But the enemy's numbers were vast. He began to be surrounded on every side. A Mughal subahdar called out—"Surrender!"

Flames blazed in Hakim Khan's eyes—"The blood of the Sur dynasty does not know how to bow!"

He spurred his horse and charged straight at the subahdar. Their swords clashed. Sparks flew. For a few moments it was as if time had stopped. Then Hakim Khan's sword found its way—the subahdar fell to the ground.

But from behind, a spear drove into his shoulder. He staggered, but did not fall. He pulled the spear out himself; blood was flowing. He looked at his army one last time—"Keep fighting!"

The Mughal soldiers fell upon him. Many blows at once. His shield broke. His sword was slipping in the blood. Still he struck one last blow—one more enemy fell.

At last he sank to his knees. All around him was a haze of dust and blood. The sun was high in the sky, but his sight was blurring. He touched the ground—as if bowing to the soil of Mewar. And then he grew still.

That day the earth of Haldighati took into itself an Afghan warrior who gave his life for the self-respect of Rajputana.

His sacrifice was not only the story of a battle, but a symbol of unity. He proved that the call of freedom goes beyond all boundaries.

Whenever the wind blows through the valley of Haldighati, the clang of swords can be heard in it. And in that clang a voice echoes—

Hakim Khan Sur.

jhala-man-singh.name: Jhala Man Singh
jhala-man-singh.story:
The ranges of the Aravallis were as unshaken that day as they had stood for centuries—but the sky of the 16th century was restless. In air heavy with the smell of dust, gunpowder and blood, a boy was born—forged in the fire of the Jhala clan, his name was Jhala Man Singh.

At the time of his birth Mewar was not just a kingdom—it was an oath of resistance. The clang of shields in the palace courtyard, the neighing of horses in the stables, and the soft whispers of battle strategy in the council halls… these were his lullabies. The Jhala clan was known for its pride, and the flame of that same pride could be seen in the boy's eyes.

From childhood it was not a wooden sword that was placed in his hands, but an edge of real steel. He would reach the stables before sunrise—stroke the horse's mane, learn its gait, then race across the open ground. His heart beat in time with the hoofbeats. As the day wore on the bowstring was drawn in his fingers, and by evening he practised with shield and sword. His teacher would tell him—"A warrior fights not only with his arms, but with his mind."

It was a time when, in the north, the Mughal empire burned with the hunger for expansion. One after another, many Rajput states were taking the path of treaty or surrender. But the throne of Mewar belonged to a name that did not know how to bow—Maharana Pratap. Around him stood a wall of loyal chiefs, and one firm pillar of that wall was Jhala Man Singh.

As he came of age his fame began to spread not only for his courage, but for his strategy too. He knew how to read a battlefield—where a hill slope could trap an enemy, where the bend of a river could stop horsemen. He trained his troops for light armour and great speed. "Strike directly only," he would say, "when the enemy is exhausted."

The first great clash came at a frontier fort. The Mughal army had planted its flag there. The fort was built on high rock, with wide flat ground in front—a direct assault would mean heavy losses. Jhala Man Singh surveyed the ground. He saw that on the western side there was a narrow pass that the guards took lightly.

The night grew deep. There was a chill in the air. Jhala signalled his small troop. Leaving their horses behind, they moved on foot towards the pass. The moon was hidden in the clouds. Suddenly he whispered—"Now."

The flash of swords cut through the darkness. The guards' screams rose. Chaos broke out inside. As soon as the Mughal soldiers posted at the main gate were distracted, the Mewari army hidden outside launched a ferocious attack. The cry of "Victory to Eklingji!" made the stones tremble. Within a few hours the fort was back in Mewar's hands.

That victory made him even dearer to the Maharana.

But that day in 1576… that day will blaze forever in the veins of history. That valley of yellow earth the colour of turmeric—Haldighati. In front, the vast sea of the Mughal army. Lines of elephants, rows of cannon, heavy cavalry. On the other side, Mewar's comparatively small army, but with fire in its eyes.

When the morning sun rose the two armies faced each other. There was an unspoken waiting in the air. Then the kettledrums sounded. A cloud of dust rose. Swords came out of their scabbards.

Maharana Pratap rode his horse Chetak. At the sight of his banner, lightning ran through the Mewari soldiers. Jhala Man Singh was close beside him—shield raised, sword gleaming.

The Mughal army fired its cannon first. The earth shook. Many Mewari soldiers fell. But Pratap spurred Chetak—straight into the heart of the enemy. Behind him Jhala Man Singh and the other chiefs charged.

The earth shook with hoofbeats. Shields clashed. Streams of blood mixed with the yellow earth to make a deeper colour. Screams, war cries, the clang of metal—all together made a terrible music.

A moment came when the Mughal army surrounded Pratap. Spears and swords rose on every side. Chetak had been wounded. Blows were landing on Pratap's armour.

Jhala Man Singh saw that scene—and in that very moment made the decision that became immortal.

He galloped to Pratap's side. He took the Rana's royal insignia—the parasol and the banner—into his own hands and called out in a loud voice—"I am Pratap!"

The Mughal soldiers' eyes turned to him. They believed he was the Maharana. They fell upon him.

He signalled Pratap to withdraw—"Rana, Mewar needs you!"

For a moment Pratap looked into his eyes. There was no fear of death there, only firm resolve.

Jhala Man Singh was now at the centre of the enemy. He swung his shield, stopped a spear, and cut down two soldiers with his sword. His horse was struck; he leapt down to the ground. Blows from every side.

With a roar of "Jhala!" he made his final attack. His sword was red with blood. He cut down a subahdar. But from behind, a spear drove into his shoulder. He sank to his knees, and still kept wielding his sword.

At last many swords fell on him at once. He fell to the earth—but the banner was still in his hand.

That day the dust of Haldighati made a sacrifice immortal.

But his life was not confined to that one moment. Before it, too, he had stopped Mughal detachments in frontier skirmishes, cut supply routes, and adopted new techniques of mountain warfare. He had taught the soldiers to split into small bands and attack without warning. He had said—"Do not count the enemy's numbers; find his weakness."

After Haldighati, Mewar's struggle went on, but the name of Jhala Man Singh had become a flame in every soldier's heart. Whenever a Rajput raised his sword, he remembered the moment when a warrior made himself the target to save his lord.

At his death even the winds of the Aravallis fell silent. When Maharana Pratap heard the news, there was both fire and anguish in his eyes. He said—"It is because of such heroes that Mewar lives."

Even today, when the sun sets over the earth of Haldighati, its colour seems deeper—as if the stream of blood from that day were still flowing there.

Jhala Man Singh is not just a name; he is the moment when duty triumphed over life. He is the roar that tells us that even death is a small price for the defence of honour.

The valleys of the Aravallis still echo—
"Mewar!"
"Victory to Eklingji!"

And in that echo one voice can always be heard—
Jhala Man Singh.

bhamashah.name: Bhamashah
bhamashah.significance: Minister and treasurer of Maharana Pratap whose wealth sustained Mewar's war
bhamashah.story:
**Bhamashah — the treasurer who saved a war**

**Bhamashah** was born on **28 June 1547** in an **Oswal Jain** family of Mewar. His father **Bharmal** had served Rana Sanga and Udai Singh II, and Bhamashah grew up close to the court. Under **Maharana Pratap** he became **pradhan**, the chief minister of Mewar.

**After Haldighati**

After the battle of **Haldighati** (1576), Pratap's war against Akbar moved into the hills. Mewar's plains were lost, its revenue was gone, and the Maharana had to keep an army alive in the forests. At this moment, tradition says, Bhamashah placed his family's entire fortune at Pratap's feet, enough, it is said, to maintain **25,000 soldiers for twelve years**. Whether or not the figure is exact, his wealth allowed Mewar to keep fighting.

**Minister and organiser**

Bhamashah was not a battlefield general but an organiser. He managed supplies, paid the soldiers and kept the accounts of a government in exile. With his brother **Tarachand**, who fought at Haldighati, he also led expeditions into Mughal-held **Malwa** to gather funds for the war. The recovery of most of Mewar in the 1580s, crowned by the victory at **Dewair**, rested in part on his work.

**Last years**

After Pratap's death in 1597, Bhamashah continued as minister under **Maharana Amar Singh I**. He died in **1600**, and his son **Jiva Shah** succeeded him as minister.

**Legacy**

In Rajasthan the name Bhamashah has become a word for a generous patron who gives everything for a great cause.

panna-dhai.name: Panna Dhai
panna-dhai.significance: Mewar nurse-martyr who saved Udai Singh
panna-dhai.story:
The ramparts of Chittor were unusually silent that night. Some unknown fear was floating in the air. That was the 16th century… Mewar was trembling from within. The shadow of treachery in the royal court, a thirst for blood in the pursuit of power, and the Mughal gaze from outside. In that darkness stood a woman—carrying no sword, wearing no armour—but with the courage of lions in her heart. She was Panna Dhai.

She was not born in a palace, but her soul was royal. From childhood she regarded service as her dharma. When she became a nurse in the palace of Mewar, she held in her hands not just a cradle, but the heartbeat of the future. The boy Udai Singh—the lamp of the Sisodia dynasty—was growing up in her lap.

Panna Dhai did not only nurse him; she told him the sagas of his line.
"This land does not bow," she would say.
The boy would look into her eyes, as if he understood.

But a storm had already risen within Mewar. Bloodthirsty hands were reaching for power. Whispers of conspiracy echoed in the palace walls. One night—deep darkness, dim lamps, and the shadow of swords.

"Banbir is coming…" a trusted servant whispered.

For a moment Panna's heart trembled, but in her eyes there was not fear, but decision. She looked at the boy Udai Singh—asleep, innocent. Then she looked at her own son—raised in the same lap, with the same light in his eyes.

Footsteps outside… the clink of swords…
"Where is the prince?" a cruel voice rang out.

In an instant Panna made her decision—the harshest decision in history. She lifted Udai Singh, placed him in a basket, and signalled a trusted servant—
"Take him now… towards the Aravallis… he must live."

Then she laid her own son down on the prince's bed. The lamp's flame trembled. The door broke. Banbir burst in—the fire of power in his eyes.

"Here is the prince!" He raised his sword.

A moment… and then the sword fell.

Panna Dhai did not close her eyes. She stood there—motionless. There was a storm in her heart, but on her face a stone-like resolve.

Blood flowed. Her son lay lifeless. But the lamp of the Sisodia dynasty was alive—moving towards the Aravallis.

In the morning the air of Chittor was heavy. Panna held her tears within. No lament, no wailing. Only one sentence—
"May Mewar live."

She passed along the hard paths of the Aravallis, protecting Udai Singh. Both the Mughals and the enemies within were active. Death was possible at every step. But within Panna, motherhood and duty to her land had become one.

One night in the forest they sensed enemy scouts. Torches gleamed in the distance. Panna told the servants—
"Put out the lamp. Make no sound."

The hoofbeats came close. The ring of swords. But the darkness covered them. By morning they had moved on in safety.

Years later, when Udai Singh sat on the throne of Mewar, behind that throne was Panna's blood—the sacrifice of her son.

She wore no armour, nor did she wield a sword on the battlefield. But her decision was more terrible than any war. By losing her son she saved Mewar.

One day someone asked her—
"How did you bear it?"
Panna said in a calm voice—
"My son is gone… but Mewar is my son."

Her last breaths were peaceful. No war drums, no battle. But her saga was engraved in the walls of Chittor.

Panna Dhai—the woman who gave up her motherhood and chose her duty to her land, who turned the course of history with her own blood, who proved that Mewar is defended not only by swords, but by sacrifice too.

Even today, when lamps are lit in the air of Chittor, a voice echoes—
"Mewar is immortal… Panna's sacrifice is immortal."

rao-amar-singh-i.name: Maharana Amar Singh I
rao-amar-singh-i.significance: Son of Maharana Pratap who fought the Mughals for eighteen years and made the treaty of 1615
rao-amar-singh-i.story:
**Maharana Amar Singh I — the long war and the hard peace**

Amar Singh was born on **16 March 1559**, the eldest son of **Maharana Pratap**. He grew up in the hills during his father's war against Akbar. At the battle of **Dewair** (1582) he is remembered for killing the Mughal commander **Sultan Khan** with a single spear-thrust that pierced both rider and horse.

**Maharana, 1597–1620**

When Pratap died in January 1597, Amar Singh became Maharana. The war did not end. **Jahangir**, who became emperor in 1605, sent army after army into Mewar: under Prince **Parvez** (1606), under **Mahabat Khan**, and under **Abdullah Khan**. Amar Singh fought them with the hill tactics his father had taught him, and Mewar held out.

**Khurram's campaign and the treaty of 1615**

In 1613 Jahangir sent Prince **Khurram** (later Shah Jahan) with a vast army. Khurram set up posts across Mewar, burned villages and cut off the hills from food. After almost twenty years of war, with his people exhausted, Amar Singh agreed to peace in **1615**.

The terms were honourable for the time: the Maharana would **never have to appear in person** at the Mughal court; his son **Karan Singh** went in his place; **Chittor** was returned to Mewar, on condition that it was not refortified. No daughter of Mewar was sent in marriage to the Mughals.

**The last years**

The treaty weighed heavily on Amar Singh. He handed the business of state to Karan Singh and spent his last years largely in retirement. He died on **26 January 1620**. Mewar remembers him both as a warrior who fought for eighteen years and as the ruler who chose to save his people from ruin.

kunwar-shakti-singh.name: Kunwar Shakti Singh
kunwar-shakti-singh.significance: Younger brother of Maharana Pratap, founder of the Shaktawat clan
kunwar-shakti-singh.story:
**Kunwar Shakti Singh — the estranged brother**

**Shakti Singh** was a son of **Maharana Udai Singh II** and a younger brother of **Maharana Pratap**. The brothers quarrelled, and tradition tells of a hunting dispute in which their swords were drawn against each other, stopped only when the family priest stepped between them and died.

**In Akbar's camp**

After the quarrel, Shakti Singh left Mewar and for some time served **Akbar**. Mewar tradition says he was with the Mughal army at the time of **Haldighati** (1576).

**The legend after Haldighati**

The most famous story about Shakti Singh, recorded by later chroniclers, tells that after the battle he saw two Mughal horsemen pursuing the wounded Pratap. Moved by the sight of his brother alone and hunted, he rode after them and killed them. When Pratap's horse **Chetak** fell, Shakti Singh gave him his own horse. The brothers were reconciled. Historians treat this as legend, but it is loved across Rajasthan.

**Return to Mewar**

After the reconciliation Shakti Singh returned to Mewar and is said to have recovered the fort of **Bhainsrorgarh** for his brother. His descendants became the **Shaktawat** clan, one of the leading houses of Mewar's nobility.

**Death**

Shakti Singh died in the 1590s. There is no reliable record of him dying in battle.

maharana-karan-singh-ii.name: Maharana Karan Singh II
maharana-karan-singh-ii.significance: Mewar ruler of the peace after 1615, who sheltered Prince Khurram and began the Jag Mandir
legends: Host of the rebel Prince Khurram
maharana-karan-singh-ii.story:
**Maharana Karan Singh II — the ruler who rebuilt Mewar**

Karan Singh was born on **7 January 1584**, the son of **Maharana Amar Singh I**. He grew up in the last years of Mewar's long war with the Mughals.

**At Jahangir's court**

Under the treaty of **1615**, the Maharana himself never had to attend the Mughal court, so the crown prince went instead. Karan Singh was received by **Jahangir** at Ajmer with great honour and given a high rank. He became the bridge between Mewar and the empire.

**Maharana, 1620–1628**

Karan Singh became Maharana in 1620. His reign was a time of peace after decades of war, and he used it to **rebuild**: villages were resettled, fields brought back into cultivation, and Udaipur grew. He strengthened the city's walls and began building on **Jag Mandir**, the island palace in Lake Pichola.

**Friend of Prince Khurram**

When **Prince Khurram** rebelled against his father Jahangir in 1622–23, Karan Singh, who had known him since the treaty years, gave him shelter in Udaipur. Tradition says the prince stayed in the island palace, and that its domed pavilion (the **Gul Mahal**) was built for him. When Khurram became emperor as **Shah Jahan** in 1628, he remembered this friendship.

**Legacy**

Karan Singh died in **1628**, the year Shah Jahan took the throne. He fought no great battles. His achievement was different: he turned the hard peace of 1615 into a time of recovery, and left Mewar stronger than he found it.

amar-singh-rathore.name: Amar Singh Rathore
amar-singh-rathore.significance: Rathore prince of Nagaur who killed the Mughal paymaster at Shah Jahan's court
legends: Passed over for the throne of Marwar
Legend of the leap from Agra Fort
amar-singh-rathore.story:
**Amar Singh Rathore — the prince who would not be insulted**

Amar Singh was the eldest son of **Raja Gaj Singh** of Marwar. But his father, displeased with his fiery temper, passed him over and named his younger son, **Jaswant Singh**, as heir. Amar Singh left Marwar and entered the service of **Shah Jahan**, who made him a high-ranking mansabdar and gave him **Nagaur**.

**The quarrel at court**

In **1644**, Amar Singh was absent from court for some time without leave, and a fine was imposed on him. The imperial paymaster, **Salabat Khan**, demanded the fine and, by tradition, insulted him in front of the court, calling him a rustic.

**25 July 1644**

Amar Singh drew his dagger and killed Salabat Khan in the presence of the emperor in the court at **Agra Fort**. He was cut down by the imperial guards on the spot. His Rathore companions, led by **Ballu Champawat** and **Bhao Singh Kumpawat**, fought their way into the fort to recover his body, and died there.

**The legend of the leap**

A popular legend says that Amar Singh escaped on horseback by leaping from the walls of Agra Fort, and that the gate called **Amar Singh Gate** is named after him. The contemporary records say he died in the court itself, but the legend of the leap lives on in ballads and plays.

**Memory**

Amar Singh Rathore became a hero of Rajasthani folk theatre (*khyal*) and song, remembered as the man who valued his honour above his life.

rao-chhatrasal-bundela.name: Rao Chhatrasal Bundela
rao-chhatrasal-bundela.significance: Founder of Bundela kingdom who resisted Mughals
rao-chhatrasal-bundela.story:
The land of Bundelkhand is a land of stone—hard, but full of fire within. The hills of the Vindhyas, the streams of the Ken and the Betwa, and between them the region where swords cut not only iron, but vows too. The 17th century… Aurangzeb on the throne of Delhi. The Mughal empire at its height. But in the shadow of every empire a spark is born. In 1649 CE a boy was born—Chhatrasal Bundela.

There was no grand celebration at his birth, but there was a strange stirring in the Bundela clan. His mother lifted the newborn in her arms and said—
"This boy will not bow."

From childhood Chhatrasal had an unusual stubbornness. Riding at five, the bow at seven, the sword at ten. Mastering his horse on the stony climbs of the Vindhyas, it was as if he were learning war from nature itself. By his youth his arm had grown so firm that his strokes were straight and decisive.

One day his teacher asked—
"What if the emperor of Delhi stands before you?"
Chhatrasal said calmly—
"Then the land of Bundelkhand will stop his feet."

As a young man he saw the strength of the Mughal army—its discipline, its cannon, its heavy infantry. But he also saw that the vaster the empire's expansion, the heavier its burden within. He swore an oath—
"Bundelkhand will be free."

The first battle was fought for a small fort. The Mughal subahdar demanded tribute and submission. Chhatrasal refused.

"Jai Bundela!"
"Har Har Mahadev!"

The hills trembled with the roar of the guns. Dust and smoke spread everywhere. Instead of fighting on open ground, Chhatrasal posted his army behind the cover of the hills.

"Draw them into the pass," his order rang out.

As soon as the Mughal army reached the narrow way, arrows and bullets rained from above. A cavalry charge from below. Swords clashed. Blood flowed over the stones.

A Mughal commander called out—
"Surrender!"
Chhatrasal roared—
"A Bundela does not know surrender!"

There was a duel. His strokes were swift. The enemy fell back.

The second battle was fiercer. This time the Mughal court sent a large army. The aim was clear—to end the Bundela rebellion.

Chhatrasal adopted guerrilla tactics. Raids on Mughal camps in the dark of night. Cutting the supply routes. Constant strikes by small troops.

One night fire blazed up in the Mughal camp. Chaos. By morning the Bundela army struck from the front. The enemy line wavered.

The third and decisive struggle took place on open ground. The two armies faced each other.

"Jai Bundelkhand!"
"Har Har Mahadev!"

The roar of cannon, the flash of swords, the hoofbeats of horses—the sky trembled. A storm of dust rose. Streams of blood began to flow.

A moment came when the Bundela army was surrounded. The soldiers began to fall back.

"Do not fall back!" Chhatrasal himself reached the front line. His sword fell like lightning. Blow after blow. The soldiers' morale returned.

He signalled the reserve. Suddenly the blow came from behind. The Mughal line began to break.

The battle went on long. At last the enemy fell back. Bundelkhand's freedom remained secure.

Chhatrasal did not only fight wars—he laid the foundations of a state. Building forts, reorganising the army, adopting new techniques of war. He turned the geographical strength of the Vindhyas into strategy.

For years the struggle went on. Sometimes open battle, sometimes guerrilla war. Aurangzeb's power was vast, but Chhatrasal's resolve was vaster still.

In the last phase of his life he was gazing at the hills of the Vindhyas. The sun was crimson.

A trusted companion asked—
"Maharaj, will the struggle ever end?"
He said in a low voice—
"As long as the fire of freedom burns, the struggle will go on."

His breath grew still, but his saga became immortal in the land of Bundelkhand.

Rao Chhatrasal Bundela—the founder who established a free kingdom even in the shadow of the Mughal empire, who chose resistance over surrender, who proved that even a land of stone can shake the walls of empire.

Even today a voice echoes in the winds of the Vindhyas—
"Bundelkhand is free."

maharao-shakti-singh-hada.name: Maharao Shakti Singh Hada
maharao-shakti-singh-hada.story:
*Historical note: No ruler of Bundi of this name is known. In Akbar's time Bundi was ruled by Rao Surjan Hada, who made terms with Akbar in 1569 after the siege of Ranthambore. Read this story as legend, not history.*

When the stream of the Chambal struck the hills of Bundi, the ring of swords could be heard in its echo. The fort of Taragarh—cleaving the clouds—was the silent sentinel of that turbulent 16th century. In the north Mughal power was growing. Akbar's armies had fixed their gaze on the states of Rajputana one by one. But Bundi—the land of the Hadas—still held firm to its honour. In that same fiery spirit a name was born—Maharao Shakti Singh Hada.

On the night of his birth rows of lamps were lit inside Taragarh. The roar of kettledrums echoed through the valleys. Weapons were offered at the temple of the clan goddess. An old bard lifted the newborn and said—
"This boy will become strength itself, true to his name."

From childhood Shakti Singh had intensity—firmness in his wrist, fire in his gaze. At five he began riding. On the stony climbs of Bundi he handled his horse as if it were his companion. At seven he drew the bowstring and the arrow flew straight to its mark. At ten the sword came into his hand—and soon became the symbol of his personality.

One day his teacher asked—
"What if the emperor's army stands before you?"
Shakti Singh replied—
"Then the land of Bundi will put it to the test."

While still young he was given the burden of rule. Bundi was under pressure. Envoys came from the Mughal court—bearing terms of treaty and subjection. Some chiefs advised—"Bow and save the kingdom."
But Shakti Singh, gripping the hilt of his sword, said—
"A kingdom saved by bowing is not a kingdom—it is a hostage."

The first great battle was fought on Bundi's border. The Mughal army advanced with heavy cannon and disciplined infantry.

"Jai Bundi!"
"Har Har Mahadev!"

The earth shook with the first roar of the guns. A cloud of dust rose. Shakti Singh spread his army behind the cover of the hills.

"Draw them into the narrow pass!" his order rang out.

As soon as the Mughal army came down into the valley, arrows and bullets rained from above. From below the Hada horsemen crashed in like lightning. Swords clashed. Spears gleamed. Blood flowed over the rocks.

A Mughal commander called out—
"Surrender!"
Shakti Singh roared—
"A Hada does not know surrender!"

There was a duel. His strokes were fast and deadly. The enemy fell back.

The second battle was fiercer. This time the Mughal army was greater in number. They issued a challenge to battle on open ground.

The battlefield filled with dust and smoke. Cannon shot fell. Horses were wounded. Soldiers fell.

Shakti Singh divided his army into three—cannon in the centre, fast cavalry on both wings. As soon as the Mughal army was entangled in the centre, the Hada bands crashed in from both sides.

The roar of "The honour of Taragarh!" rang out.

The earth shook with hoofbeats. The Mughal line wavered. Streams of blood began to flow.

The third and decisive struggle came when a harsh message arrived from the Mughal court—Bundi was to be brought under complete subjection.

Banners flew on the ramparts of Taragarh. Shakti Singh said in the council—
"Today it is a question of honour, greater than life."

The battlefield was wide. The two armies faced each other.

"Har Har Mahadev!"
"Jai Hada!"

The roar of cannon, the clash of swords, the hoofbeats of horses—the sky trembled. A storm of dust covered everything.

A moment came when the Mughal army tightened its ring. Bundi's front line began to fall back.

"Do not fall back!" Shakti Singh himself reached the front line. His sword fell like lightning. Blow after blow. The soldiers' morale returned.

He signalled the reserve. Suddenly the blow came from behind. The Mughal line began to break. The encirclement was reversed.

The battle went on long. But in the final stage a heavy blow tore through his shoulder. Blood flowed. His horse staggered. He fell to the ground, but the sword did not leave his hand.

A Mughal commander called out—
"There is still time—surrender!"
Shakti Singh said, his voice soaked in blood—
"A Hada… does not surrender…"

He raised his sword one last time and struck. Then his arm went slack.

The wind of the Chambal was heavy that day. Bundi lost a lion, but saved its honour.

Maharao Shakti Singh Hada—the ruler who kept Bundi unshaken even before Mughal power, who chose a hero's death over surrender, who proved that freedom beats in Hada blood until the last breath.

Even today the wind echoes over the ramparts of Taragarh—
"Bundi did not bow… and it never will."

kunwar-jagmal.name: Kunwar Jagmal
kunwar-jagmal.significance: Udai Singh II's chosen heir, set aside for Pratap, who joined Akbar and died at Datani
kunwar-jagmal.story:
**Kunwar Jagmal — the heir who was set aside**

Jagmal was a son of **Maharana Udai Singh II** by his favourite queen, **Dheer Bai Bhatiyani**. Under her influence, Udai Singh named Jagmal as his successor, passing over his eldest son, **Pratap**.

**Gogunda, 1572**

When Udai Singh died at **Gogunda** in 1572, Jagmal took his seat on the throne. But the great nobles of Mewar, among them **Krishnadas Chundawat** and **Rawat Sanga**, refused to accept him. Mewar faced the might of Akbar, and they wanted a leader who could stand against it. They led Jagmal from the throne and crowned **Pratap** in his place.

**In Akbar's service**

Humiliated, Jagmal left Mewar and went to **Akbar**, who welcomed a rival claimant to Mewar. He received the jagir of **Jahazpur**, and later Akbar gave him half of the state of **Sirohi**, setting him against its ruler, **Rao Surtan Deora**.

**Datani, 1583**

In **1583**, Jagmal marched with an imperial force against Rao Surtan. At the battle of **Datani**, Surtan's men won a famous victory, and Jagmal was killed fighting on the Mughal side.

**Memory**

Mewar's tradition remembers Jagmal as the prince who chose ambition over his homeland. His story is also a reminder of how the decision of the nobles at Gogunda changed history: without it there would have been no Maharana Pratap.

rao-ratan-singh-rathore.name: Raja Ratan Singh Rathore of Ratlam
rao-ratan-singh-rathore.significance: Founder of Ratlam state, killed at Dharmat fighting for the imperial side
legends: Hero of the Dingal poem Ratan Rasau
rao-ratan-singh-rathore.story:
**Raja Ratan Singh Rathore — the founder of Ratlam**

Ratan Singh was born in **1618** into a branch of the **Rathores of Marwar**, descended from **Raja Udai Singh** of Jodhpur. He served the Mughal emperor **Shah Jahan** with distinction, and in **1652** Shah Jahan granted him the territory of **Ratlam** in Malwa. He became the founder of the Ratlam state.

**The legend of the elephant**

A well-known story tells that a mad imperial elephant ran amok in Agra, and Ratan Singh faced it alone on horseback, striking it down while the court watched. The story made his name famous across the empire.

**Dharmat, 1658**

In the war of succession, Shah Jahan sent **Maharaja Jaswant Singh** of Marwar, with Ratan Singh among the Rajput commanders, to stop **Aurangzeb** and **Murad**. At **Dharmat**, near Ujjain, in April 1658, the Rajputs charged into the princes' guns. When the battle turned, Ratan Singh refused to leave the field and was killed fighting, loyal to the emperor he served.

**The poem of his death**

The Charan poet **Khidiya Jaga** celebrated his last stand in the Dingal poem *Vachanika Rathor Ratan Singh ji ri*, also called the *Ratan Rasau*, one of the finest works of Dingal literature. His descendants ruled Ratlam until 1948.

rawat-kesri-singh.name: Rawat Kesri Singh
rawat-kesri-singh.significance: Mewar warrior who fought at Haldighati
rawat-kesri-singh.story:
*Historical note: No warrior of this name is found in the historical accounts of Haldighati. Read this story as legend, not history.*

When the yellow earth of the Aravallis is ground beneath swords, it becomes Haldighati—a land coloured with blood and vows. That was the 16th century… the Mughal empire was expanding its power. Akbar's armies were disciplined, his artillery fearsome, and his strategy far-reaching. But Mewar—the land that had seen the flames of jauhar and had saved its pride even while eating bread made of grass—still stood firm. In that same unshaken tradition a name was born—Rawat Kesri Singh.

He was born into the heroic tradition of the Sisodia dynasty. He was named amid the worship of weapons at the temple of the clan goddess—Kesri, the lion. As the lion, so was his nature. From childhood there was an extraordinary flame in his eyes. At five he began riding. He raced his horse without fear over the stony slopes of the Aravallis. At seven the bowstring was drawn. At ten the sword became an extension of his arm.

One day his teacher asked—
"What if the enemy is twice our number?"
Kesri Singh replied—
"Then our courage will be four times greater."

While still young he swore an oath to serve Mewar. It was a time when Maharana Pratap stood unshaken before Mughal power. Offers of treaty and subjection had been rejected. Conflict was inevitable.

The valley of Haldighati—yellow earth, narrow passes, mountains on both sides. The Mughal army vast, equipped with cannon and cavalry. Mewar's army fewer in number, but boundless in spirit.

Before the battle the Maharana said—
"Today the honour of Mewar rests on the edge of the sword."

Rawat Kesri Singh stood in the front line. There was fire in his eyes.

"Victory to Eklingnath!"
"Mewar is immortal!"

The valley trembled with the first roar of the guns. A cloud of dust rose. The Mughal army advanced. Kesri Singh posted his band behind the cover of the hills.

"As soon as they are entangled in the centre—charge!" he ordered.

The Mughal army struck at the centre. At that very moment Kesri Singh and his horsemen crashed in like lightning. Swords clashed. Spears gleamed. Blood sank into the turmeric earth.

A Mughal chief challenged him—
"Bow!"
Kesri Singh roared—
"A Sisodia does not bow!"

There was a duel. Blow after blow. His strike was deadly. The enemy fell back, but their numbers were heavy.

The battle grew fiercer. Maharana Pratap himself rode Chetak into the midst of the enemy. At that moment Kesri Singh was beside him—like a shield.

The second assault came after noon. The Mughal army tried to tighten its ring. Kesri Singh sensed the situation.

"Push the right wing forward! Let them spread out!" his order rang out.

The strategy worked. Disorder spread through the Mughal line. But with the thunder of cannon and muskets, many heroes of Mewar fell.

In the third phase the battle reached its height. The valley was filled with blood. Horses wounded, soldiers exhausted, but morale unshaken.

A trusted companion called out—
"Rawat Sahab, fall back!"
He replied—
"Falling back is the last resort!"

He spurred his horse into the midst of the enemy. His sword fell like lightning. Many Mughal soldiers fell. But a musket ball tore through his shoulder. Blood flowed, but he did not stop.

A Mughal commander called out—
"There is still time—surrender!"
Kesri Singh said, his mouth wet with blood—
"Surrender… never…"

He raised his sword one last time and struck. Then another blow landed on his chest. He fell to the ground, but the sword did not leave his hand.

That day the yellow earth of Haldighati grew deeper in colour—with blood.

Rawat Kesri Singh—the Sisodia warrior who faced the Mughals shoulder to shoulder with Maharana Pratap at Haldighati, who chose a hero's death over surrender, who proved that the honour of Mewar is greater than death.

Even today, when dust rises in the air of Haldighati, a voice echoes in it—
"Mewar is immortal… the Sisodias stand unshaken."

rao-surtan-singh.name: Rao Surtan Deora
rao-surtan-singh.significance: Deora Chauhan ruler of Sirohi who defied Akbar and won the battle of Datani
rao-surtan-singh.story:
**Rao Surtan Deora — the defiant lord of Sirohi**

**Rao Surtan** belonged to the **Deora** branch of the **Chauhans**, who ruled **Sirohi** in the hills of south-western Rajasthan, around **Mount Abu**. He came to the throne as a boy in **1571** and ruled for almost forty years.

**Between Mewar and the Mughals**

Sirohi lay between Mewar, Marwar and Gujarat, on the road the Mughal armies used. Like his neighbour **Maharana Pratap**, Surtan refused to accept Akbar's authority. Akbar tried to break him by supporting his rivals: he gave half of Sirohi to **Jagmal**, the half-brother of Maharana Pratap who had joined the Mughals.

**Datani, 1583**

In **October 1583**, Jagmal and an imperial force, joined by **Raisingh**, a son of Rao Chandrasen of Marwar, marched against Surtan. At **Datani**, near Sirohi, Surtan's Deoras won a complete victory. Both Jagmal and Raisingh were killed. The battle became famous in the songs of the Charans.

**The long defiance**

Tradition credits Surtan with fighting more than fifty battles. He kept Sirohi largely independent, and late in his reign came to terms with the Mughals without losing his state. He died in **1610**.

**Memory**

Rao Surtan is remembered as one of the Rajput rulers who, like Pratap, refused to bow to Akbar, and the hills of Sirohi and Abu still keep the memory of Datani.

durgadas-rathore.name: Durgadas Rathore
durgadas-rathore.significance: Legendary Rathore warrior who saved Marwar
durgadas-rathore.story:
Even when the nights of the desert were sunk in silence, a story echoed among the grains of sand—a story of vengeance, vow and resistance. The Marwar of the 17th century… Aurangzeb on the throne of Delhi, his ambition boundless, his army vast. Mehrangarh fort in Jodhpur touching the sky, but surrounded by the shadow of Mughal power. At such a time, in 1638 CE, a boy was born—Durgadas Rathore.

There was no royal celebration at his birth, but a wave of pride ran through the Rathore clan. An old bard looked at the infant and said—
"Like his name, this boy will be a fortress—impregnable."

From childhood Durgadas had extraordinary resolve. When he sat on a horse at five, he gripped the reins tight. Racing over the sand dunes, he learned balance. The bow at seven, the sword at ten. By his youth his wrist had such strength that his strokes were straight and merciless.

One day his teacher asked—
"What if the emperor himself stands before you?"
Durgadas replied—
"Then the sword will speak."

Time soon tested him. Marwar was in crisis. After Maharaja Jaswant Singh, the Mughal court tried to bring Marwar under its control. A plan was made to seize Jodhpur. But Rathore blood was boiling.

Durgadas swore an oath—
"I will not let Marwar bow."

The first great struggle took place near Jodhpur. The Mughal army was disciplined, equipped with cannon.

"Jai Marwar!"
"The honour of the Rathores!"

The earth shook with the roar of the guns. Instead of meeting them head-on in the open, Durgadas spread his army among the dunes.

"The sand is our shield," his order rang out.

As soon as the Mughal army advanced, horsemen hidden behind the dunes suddenly crashed in. A rain of arrows and bullets. Swords clashed. Blood sank into the sand.

A Mughal commander called out—
"Surrender!"
Durgadas roared—
"A Rathore does not know surrender!"

There was a duel. His strokes were swift and unerring. The enemy fell back.

The second battle was fiercer. The Mughal court sent a vast army. The aim was clear—to bring Marwar under complete subjection.

Durgadas adopted a new strategy—guerrilla war. Raids on Mughal camps in the dark of night. Attacks on supply routes. Driving off horses, disabling cannon.

One night fire blazed up in the Mughal camp. Chaos. By morning the army of Marwar struck from the front. The enemy line wavered.

The third and decisive struggle took place on open ground. The two armies faced each other.

"Har Har Mahadev!"
"Jai Marwar!"

The roar of cannon, the flash of swords, the hoofbeats of horses—the sky trembled. A storm of dust rose. Streams of blood began to flow.

A moment came when the Mughal army tightened its ring. Marwar's front line began to fall back.

"Do not fall back!" Durgadas himself reached the front line. His sword fell like lightning. Blow after blow. The soldiers' morale returned.

He signalled the reserve. Suddenly the blow came from behind. The Mughal line began to break. The encirclement was reversed.

The battle went on long. At last the enemy was forced to fall back.

Durgadas did not only fight wars—he strengthened Marwar from within. Repairing forts, reorganising the army, adopting new techniques of war. He turned the geographical strength of the desert into strategy.

For years the struggle went on. Sometimes open battle, sometimes guerrilla raids. Aurangzeb's power was vast, but Durgadas's resolve was vaster still.

In the last days of his life he was gazing at the horizon of the desert. The sun was crimson. The sand was still.

A trusted companion asked—
"Thakur Sahab, is Marwar safe?"
Durgadas said in a low voice—
"As long as there is fire in Rathore blood, Marwar will live."

His breath grew still, but his saga still echoes in the storms of the desert.

Durgadas Rathore—the warrior who kept Marwar unshaken even before Mughal power, who chose resistance over surrender, who proved that the Rathore line can save its freedom even on the edge of the sword.

Even today a voice rises in the air of the desert—
"The honour of the Rathores is immortal."

maharaja-jaswant-singh.name: Maharaja Jaswant Singh
maharaja-jaswant-singh.significance: Rathore ruler of Marwar and senior Mughal mansabdar, scholar and poet
maharaja-jaswant-singh.story:
**Maharaja Jaswant Singh — the Rathore between two worlds**

Jaswant Singh was born on **26 December 1626** at **Burhanpur**, the son of **Maharaja Gaj Singh** of Marwar. He became ruler of Marwar in **1638**, at the age of eleven, and, like his father, served the Mughal emperors as a high-ranking **mansabdar**.

**Dharmat, 1658**

In the war of succession, Shah Jahan sent Jaswant Singh to stop **Aurangzeb** and **Murad**. At **Dharmat**, near Ujjain, in April 1658, the Rathores charged with great courage, but the princes' artillery and numbers carried the day. Jaswant Singh returned to Jodhpur defeated. Tradition says his queen, a Hada princess, closed the gates of the fort against him, saying a Rajput should return victorious or not at all.

**A dangerous game**

After Aurangzeb's victory, Jaswant Singh submitted to him. At **Khajwa** (January 1659), during Aurangzeb's battle against Shuja, he turned against him and plundered the imperial camp. He then promised to join Dara, but was persuaded by **Mirza Raja Jai Singh** to stay away, and Dara was defeated at **Deorai** alone. Aurangzeb forgave him, but never trusted him.

**In imperial service**

Jaswant Singh served in the **Deccan** against Shivaji, as governor of **Gujarat**, and finally on the north-western frontier. He died at **Jamrud**, near the Khyber Pass, on **28 November 1678**.

**Scholar and poet**

Jaswant Singh was also a scholar. His *Bhasha Bhushan* is a classic work on Hindi poetics, and he wrote on Vedanta philosophy.

**After his death**

Aurangzeb took Marwar under direct control. The struggle to save Jaswant Singh's posthumous son, **Ajit Singh**, led by **Durgadas Rathore**, became the great Rathore war of 1679–1707.

maharana-raj-singh.name: Maharana Raj Singh
maharana-raj-singh.story:
The ranges of the Aravallis were not just mountains then—they were a shield. The lakes of Mewar were not just water—they were the eyes of history, which had seen the flames of jauhar, bread made of grass, and battlefields stained with blood. The 17th century… Aurangzeb sat on the throne of Delhi. His empire was vast, his policies harsh, his sword merciless. But Mewar—the land of Sisodia blood—still stood firm. In that same unshaken tradition, in 1629 CE, a boy was born—Maharana Raj Singh.

On the night of his birth rows of lamps were lit in the temple of Eklingnath. The war drum sounded. An old bard looked at the newborn's brow and said—
"In times of crisis this boy will roar like a lion."

From childhood Raj Singh had a unique resolve. When he was put on a horse at five, he held the reins as if he had been a warrior from birth. He raced without fear up the rugged climbs of the Aravallis. The bow at seven, the sword at ten. By his youth his arm had such strength that his strokes were straight and deadly.

One day his teacher asked—
"What if Aurangzeb comes himself with an army?"
Raj Singh replied, calm but firm—
"Then the Aravallis will become his grave."

While still young he received the throne of Mewar. The kingdom was under pressure. Mughal subahdars came with demands of tribute, subjection and humiliating terms. Many states had already bowed. But in the Sisodia tradition, bowing was the last resort—and even then only at the cost of one's life.

The first great battle took place in a frontier pass. The Mughal army advanced with heavy cannon and disciplined infantry.

"Victory to Eklingnath!"
"Mewar is immortal!"

The earth shook with the first roar of the guns. Smoke spread everywhere. Raj Singh withdrew his army from the open ground and posted it in the hills.

"Let them come into the narrow way," his order rang out.

As soon as the enemy entered the pass, arrows and bullets rained from above. A cavalry charge from below. Swords clashed. Blood flowed over the stones.

A Mughal commander called out—
"Bow, and live!"
Raj Singh roared—
"A Sisodia's life is freedom!"

There was a duel. His strokes were swift and unerring. The enemy fell back.

The second battle was fiercer. Aurangzeb sent a harsh order—Mewar was to be brought under complete subjection. This time the army was vast. Cannon, cavalry, infantry—all organised.

The blow fell in the direction of Udaipur. The ramparts of the forts shook. Stones broke. Soldiers inside were wounded.

A general said—
"Maharana, their numbers are double ours."
Raj Singh replied—
"Then our courage will be four times greater."

In the dark of night guerrilla troops went out. Fire suddenly broke out in the Mughal camp. Supply stores burned. Chaos among the horses. By morning the army of Mewar struck from the front. The enemy line wavered.

The third and decisive struggle took place on open ground. The two armies faced each other. Banners flew in the wind.

"Har Har Mahadev!"
"The honour of Mewar!"

The roar of cannon, the flash of swords, the hoofbeats of horses—the sky trembled. A storm of dust rose. Streams of blood began to flow.

A moment came when the Mughal army tightened its ring. Mewar's front line began to fall back.

"Do not fall back!" Raj Singh himself reached the front line. His sword flashed like lightning. Blow after blow. The soldiers' morale returned.

He signalled the reserve. Suddenly the blow came from behind. The Mughal line began to break. The encirclement was reversed.

The battle went on long. By sunset the Mughal army was forced to fall back.

Raj Singh did not only fight wars—he strengthened Mewar from within. Repairing forts, expanding the artillery, training musketeers. Adopting new techniques of war. Organising supply and communications. He made the Aravallis his shield.

For years the struggle went on. Sometimes open battle, sometimes guerrilla raids. Aurangzeb's power was vast, but Mewar's resolve was unshaken.

In the last days of his life Raj Singh stood on the shore of the lake at Udaipur. The sun was crimson. The Aravallis were silent.

A trusted companion asked—
"Maharana, will Aurangzeb ever bow?"
Looking towards the horizon, Raj Singh said—
"Bowing is not his way… but it is not ours either."

Some time later his breath grew still. But his roar still echoes in the valleys of the Aravallis.

Maharana Raj Singh—the Sisodia ruler who kept Mewar unshaken even before Aurangzeb's harsh policies, who chose resistance over surrender, who proved that freedom can live even on the edge of the sword.

Even today a voice rises in the winds of the Aravallis—
"Mewar did not bow… and it never will."

rana-jai-singh-i.name: Mirza Raja Jai Singh I
rana-jai-singh-i.significance: Kachwaha ruler of Amber and one of the greatest Mughal generals
rana-jai-singh-i.story:
**Mirza Raja Jai Singh I — the general of three emperors**

Jai Singh was born on **15 July 1611** into the **Kachwaha** house of **Amber**. He became Raja in **1621**, when he was only about ten years old, and spent the rest of his life in the service of the Mughal empire.

**A soldier of the empire**

Under **Jahangir** and **Shah Jahan** he fought in almost every corner of the empire: in the Deccan, in Central Asia at **Balkh**, and in the campaigns for **Kandahar**. Shah Jahan gave him the title **Mirza Raja**, a mark of the highest favour.

**The war of succession**

In 1658 Jai Singh was sent east with Dara Shikoh's son **Sulaiman Shikoh**, and defeated Prince **Shah Shuja** at **Bahadurpur**. When Dara lost at Samugarh, Jai Singh judged that his cause was finished and went over to **Aurangzeb**. Before the battle of **Deorai** (1659) his letters persuaded **Jaswant Singh of Marwar** not to join Dara.

**Purandar, 1665**

Aurangzeb sent Jai Singh against **Shivaji**. Combining siege-craft and diplomacy, he besieged **Purandar** and made Shivaji accept the **Treaty of Purandar** (June 1665), giving up 23 forts. He persuaded Shivaji to visit Aurangzeb at Agra in 1666, guaranteeing his safety; Shivaji's escape from Agra, under the watch of Jai Singh's son **Ram Singh**, cost the Kachwahas Aurangzeb's trust.

**The end**

Jai Singh's campaign against **Bijapur** in 1666 failed. Recalled and out of favour, he died at **Burhanpur** on **28 August 1667**.

*Note: the "scientist-king" of Amber who built the Jantar Mantar observatories was a later ruler, **Sawai Jai Singh II** (1688–1743).*

kunwar-prithviraj-singh.name: Kunwar Prithviraj Singh
kunwar-prithviraj-singh.story:
*Historical note: No prince of this name fighting these wars is found in the historical record. Read this story as legend, not history.*

When the ramparts of Amber fort, set on the eastern arms of the Aravallis, put on a red glow in the morning sun, it seemed as if the stones themselves were stained with blood. That was the 17th century—when the Mughal emperor on the throne of Delhi wanted to push the borders of his empire further still. His army disciplined, his cannon thundering, and his intent unshakeable. But Amber—the land of the Kachwahas—stood firm with its pride. In that land a prince was born—Kunwar Prithviraj Singh.

On the night of his birth rows of lamps were lit in Amber fort. Kettledrums boomed. Prayers were offered at the temple of the clan goddess. An old bard looked at the infant's brow and said—
"This boy will be a thunderbolt on the battlefield."

From childhood Prithviraj Singh had a remarkable balance in his nature—calm, but with fire within. At five he began riding. He raced without fear over the stony slopes of Amber. At seven the bowstring thrummed at his touch. At ten the sword came into his hand, and soon its turning in his wrist became an art.

One day his teacher asked—
"What if the emperor's army stands before you?"
The prince replied firmly—
"The emperor's sword is made of steel, and my resolve is harder still."

While still young he saw the bitterness of politics. The Mughal subahdars wanted to impose terms of subjection and tribute on Amber. Some courtiers suggested compromise. But within Prithviraj burned the heat of Kachwaha blood.

The first great battle took place on Amber's border. The Mughal army advanced with heavy cannon and infantry.

"Jai Amber!"
"Har Har Mahadev!"

The earth shook with the first roar of the guns. A cloud of smoke rose. Kunwar Prithviraj posted his army on the hills.

"Entangle them on the heights," his order rang out.

As soon as the Mughal army entered the narrow way, arrows and bullets rained from above. A cavalry charge from below. Swords clashed. Blood flowed over the stones.

A Mughal commander called out—
"Bow, and live!"
Prithviraj roared—
"A Kachwaha does not know how to bow!"

There was a duel. His strokes were swift and unerring. The enemy fell back.

The second battle took place on open ground. This time the Mughal army was greater in number. The cannon were thundering.

The battlefield filled with dust and smoke.

With a roar of "The honour of Amber!" the Kachwaha horsemen charged.

A moment came when Amber's front line wavered.

"Do not fall back!" The prince himself reached the front line. His sword flashed like lightning. The soldiers' morale returned.

He adopted a new strategy—pushing the right wing forward and drawing the left back to try to encircle the enemy. The Mughal army was confused. As soon as it was caught in the ring, its line began to break.

The battle went on until sunset. At last the enemy fell back.

The third and decisive struggle came when a harsh order arrived from the Mughal court—Amber would have to bow.

Prithviraj stood up in the court.
"Today it is not only the kingdom, but our tradition that is at stake."

The battlefield was wide. The two armies faced each other.

"Har Har Mahadev!"
"Jai Amber!"

The roar of cannon, the hoofbeats of horses, the clash of swords—the sky trembled.

The battle was terrible. Streams of blood were flowing. A moment came when the enemy tightened its ring.

A trusted companion called out—
"Kunwar Sahab, fall back!"
He roared—
"A Kachwaha does not retreat!"

He spurred his horse into the midst of the enemy. His sword took many blows and gave many. But at last a deep wound struck his chest.

Blood flowed. His horse staggered. He fell to the ground, but the sword did not leave his hand.

A Mughal commander said—
"There is still time—surrender!"
Lying on the blood-soaked earth, Prithviraj replied—
"Surrender… never…"

He raised his sword one last time and struck. Then his arm went slack.

The land of Amber lost a prince, but saved its honour.

Kunwar Prithviraj Singh—the Kachwaha prince who refused to bow even before Mughal power, who gave his life on the battlefield, who proved that Amber's freedom could live even on the edge of the sword.

Even today, when the wind echoes over the ramparts of Amber, one voice can be heard in it—
"The honour of the Kachwahas is immortal."

rao-amar-singh-ii.name: Maharana Amar Singh II
rao-amar-singh-ii.significance: Mewar ruler who reorganised the nobility and allied with Marwar and Amber in 1708
legends: Alliance of 1708 with Marwar and Amber
rao-amar-singh-ii.story:
**Maharana Amar Singh II — the organiser**

Amar Singh was born on **3 October 1672**, the son of **Maharana Jai Singh** of Mewar. As a young prince he lived through Mewar's war with **Aurangzeb** after 1679, which ended in an uneasy peace in 1681.

**Maharana, 1698–1710**

Amar Singh became Maharana in **1698**. Mewar was exhausted, and he set out to strengthen it from within. He **reorganised the ranks of the nobility**, fixing the grades of the great nobles and their duties of service, a system that shaped Mewar's court for generations. He worked to restore agriculture and the revenue of the state.

**The alliance of 1708**

After Aurangzeb's death in 1707, the new emperor **Bahadur Shah I** tried to keep **Marwar** and **Amber** under Mughal control. In **1708**, **Ajit Singh** of Marwar and **Sawai Jai Singh II** of Amber came to Udaipur, and Amar Singh made an alliance with them. With Mewar's support, both recovered their capitals. To seal the alliance Amar Singh gave his daughter in marriage to Jai Singh II, on the condition that her son would succeed in Amber, a condition that later caused bitter conflict in Jaipur.

**Legacy**

Amar Singh II died on **10 December 1710**. He fought no famous battle, but the alliance of 1708 was the last time the three great Rajput houses stood together against the empire.

kunwar-bhim-singh.name: Kunwar Bhim Singh
kunwar-bhim-singh.significance: Mewar prince who died fighting Mughals
kunwar-bhim-singh.story:
Kunwar Bhim Singh was a warrior prince of the Sisodia dynasty of Mewar who touched the very height of valour while still young. Born into the royal family of Mewar, Bhim Singh was familiar from childhood with the edge of the sword and the dust of the battlefield. His teachers taught him the spirit of valour and duty that had kept Mewar unconquered for centuries.
When Mughal forces advanced on Mewar, Bhim Singh, despite his youth, took his place in the front line of the army. On the battlefield his sword worked like lightning. His daring deeds lifted the morale of the whole army. In one battle, when the general was wounded, Bhim Singh took command himself. Mounted on his horse, he crashed into the enemy lines. The enemy soldiers could not stand before him.
But this battle was Bhim Singh's last. A grievous blow laid him on the ground. Yet before he fell he had already sent several Mughal chiefs to their deaths. His death carried a message to Mewar's army to press forward.
Even today the name of Kunwar Bhim Singh is spoken with pride in Mewar. He was a ray of the flame of Mewar's valour, which will burn for centuries.
